subsubtopic: EXPLANATION OF THE INCIDENT REGARDING MR. IRVINE'S BILL
speechtext:
I wish to read to the House the following letter which I have received from the chief of the Orders and Notices branch concerning the incident which occurred yesterday with respect to Mr. Irvine's bill to amend the Criminal Code:
February 22nd, 1923.
Honourable Rodolphe Lemieux,
The Speaker,
House of Commons.
Honourable and Dear Sir,	-
The incident regarding Mr. Irvine's bill to amend the Criminal Code seems to be the outcome of some very natural misunderstanding on the part of some person. On the 31st January last I received from Mr. Irvine a written order to place a bill bearing that title upon the Order Paper. I did so; thus far there does not apear to be any difficulty. On the 8th February I received, from the Assistant Clerk, a written order to place upon the Order Paper a bill, also in Mr. Irvine's name, and bearing the same title; that is to say "An Act to amend the Criminal Code." I hold both of the above-mentioned orders. The latter one came out to me from the House, I had no discretion in the matter; all I had to do was to place it on the Order Paper as directed. It might have been a bill to amend some other provision of the Criminal Code, that Mr. Irvine desired to introduce. In any case I could do nothing other than follow my instructions. I did so, as I have always done, to the best of my ability, and I beg to express my regret that any misunderstanding should have arisen.
I have the honour to be, Honourable and Dear Sir, Yours very respectfully,
H. Crossley Sherwood,
Chief of Orders and Notices Branch.

The House resumed from Friday, February 16, the debate on the motion of Mr. Power (Quebec South).
That in the opinion of this House, it is advisable to repeal chapter 12, 8-9 George V., an Act respecting the Civil Service of Canada.
Mr. JOS. T. SHAW (Calgary West): Before resuming the discussion on the important resolution proposed by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), I would like to indicate my appreciation of his courage, and also of his frankness, in presenting this resolution for our consideration. There can be no question in the mind of the hon. member as to what he proposes to do with the Civil Service.
I would also like to say a word or two with regard to the attitude assumed by the seconder of that resolution (Mr. Chevrier). While, apparently, he had in his mind some slight reservation with regard to seconding the proposed resolution, yet upon further consideration, and certainly in view of his arguments, there can be no reason to my mind why he should make any mental reservation whatsoever. I do not wish for a moment to misrepresent the attitude of the seconder of the resolution in any way, but if I understand his position correctly it is simply this: He desires that technical officers in the Civil Service shall be removed entirely from the jurisdiction of the commission. He asks further that those engaged in what he calls "labour" shall be removed from the jurisdiction of that body. In the third place, he asks if I understand
The Civil Service

him'correotly, that the so-called clerical positions shall be removed from the jurisdiction of the commission so far as regards appointment and promotion, and of course, pay. In other words, if the seconder of the resolution had his wish, he would simply permit the Civil Service Commission to hold testing examinations with regard to the clerical staff of the Civil Service. I think, therefore, that upon mature consideration that hon. gentleman should have no difficulty whatever in seconding unreservedly the resolution of the hon. member for Quebec South.
The seconder also dwelt at some length-not only the other day but on the occasion of the debate last year-on, what he was pleased to call the "joke book" consisting, I understand, of some two or three volumes. Now I do not know very much about this joke book, but I do know that the classifications made therein have meant considerable sums of money to those employed in the Civil Service, and quite properly I think, and if I judge the attitude of civil servants correctly I think perhaps they would appreciate another joke book rather than have the one already existing removed.
I would like to say that I have listened with considerable care to the arguments which have been advanced, and I notice that every single argument presented during this debate, and also last year, was made without avail, over fifty years ago at the time the merit system was introduced into the English Civil Service. At that time it was urged that the proposed commission was altogether too expensive, that it was a great patronage bureau, and it was urged at that time* just as it is to-day, that it would take away the responsibility of the ministry. So that even in those days in England, fifty years ago, when civil service reform was in its very swaddling clothes, it was suggested by politicians that the constitution of this commission simply meant the creation of a bureaucracy with a resultant loss of esprit de corps in the service. But the lapse of time and the development of a very sane and alert public opinion in England have freed that service from partisanship and from political control and has made it what it is to-day, a service which is at once the envy and the admiration of every civilized country in the world.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Is it not a fact that for
several years after the passage of the first civil service reform bill in England a large number of amendments thereto were introduced and carried in order to bring it to its present workable condition?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
I think that exactly the same situation developed there as has developed
	,
here. The appointment of that commission was opposed by political influences of various kinds from time to time, and efforts were made every now and then to put it on a somewhat different basis. It was attacked from every possible angle, as the same reform has been attacked in this country. Our Civil Service Commission is going through its testing time just as the Civil Service Commission in England went through its period of trial. Our commission has been established somewhat less than five years and one cannot reasonably expect that you can build a structure which is perfect in every part and develop it to its fullest extent within that time, especially when one realizes that in order to do that you must uproot convictions which have been deeply laid as a result of a spoils system in force for approximately fifty years in Canada. In our country patronage has ever been the mainspring of political parties; and it cannot be expected that party adherents so recently divorced from these accepted privileges should now stand idly by and allow themselves to be permanently deprived of its control and exercise. Until 1908 patronage flourished in this country. Following the advent of every new government there" were hundreds of dismissals for which no reason whatsoever was given except mere political partisanship. Then followed in due course a long series of parliamentary debates, most acrimonious in their character, charges first by one party and then by another-debates which I humbly suggest did not in any way raise the dignity of parliament, but which on the contrary demoralized the Civil Service, because it was dragged through the mire of fierce partisan controversy.
I want to catalogue very shortly some of the admitted abuses which ensued as a result of that system. There was first of all the waste of public money. I believe that one of the auditors general of this country stated on one occasion that if he were given one-third of the money expended on the Civil Service he would be able to create a more efficient service than was then in operation. Not only has there been a waste of public money, however, but there has been a waste in human efficiency, because, owing to the fact that priority was given to political friends largely without consideration of merit, and owing to the insecurity of tenure which necessarily attended appointments, and the necessity, on the part of civil servants, of constantly having a friend at court in order to maintain positions secured, it followed that the Civil Service was bound to be demoralized and inefficient. Then unfortunately-and per-

The Civil Service
haps this is one of the most important incidents of the system-was the fact that the public morals were corrupted. People were debauched largely with their own money, and the promise of the bestowal of public office resulted too frequently in influencing elections held in tins country. Now, I suggest to hon. members that no one escaped the baneful influences of this patronage system, nor did any one in the long run profit by it. Under these circumstances one is not in the least surprised that there was a lowered morale in the public service, that there was a lack of economy, and consequently a lack of efficiency. I am not suggesting that the Liberal party was more to blame than the Conservative party; I think they were equally to blame. Not only that; if any other party had been in power at that time they would have followed in the wake of both old parties and adapted themselves to the then existing evils. But fortunately the public itself began to realize the necessity for reform. Governments, too, were not unmindful of the situation, because they appreciated the fact that this patronage system was the mightiest engine that made for the destruction of governments. Besides, members of parliament, I think, also began to realize that the dispensing of patronage was not the pleasant duty which it was sometimes considered to be. And, as a fact, many more people were disappointed than could possibly have their desires gratified by appointment to the Civil Service. As a result of this combination of forces directed towards reform, in 1908 a merit system was to some slight extent introduced into the Civil Service. That measure of civil service reform applied only to the inside service; it applied only to about 2,200 employees in Ottawa. However, despite the introduction of that partial reform, I do not think it can be urged with entire truth that even in that part of the service to which the reform applied patronage was dispensed with, because the peculiar method that was adopted resulted many times, I understand, in political friends receiving preferment. In 1911, we had another change of government. I glanced casually through the debates that took place in parliament, to see to what extent dismissals had occurred following the advent of the new government; and I found some fifty or sixty pages of Hansard indicating wholesale dismissals from the service. There can be no doubt that after that election, with the change of government it brought, the Civil Service had a distinctly Conservative hue. The war brought in its train many evils, but it also brought many things of very great value, one of which was
the crystallization in the public mind of the necessity for a more complete measure of civil service reform. And so, as a result of a definite mandate from the people in 1917, civil service reform was introduced by the Union government. The Civil Service Act was passed in 1918 and stands to-day subject to the amendments that have been made in the interim. I would point this out particularly, that there has been no mandate from the public of this country asking for a return to the patronage system. Now, the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), who moved the resolution, suggested with some degree of fervour that the Civil Service Commission, as constituted under the Civil Service Act, in some way thwarted responsible government, and was to that extent at least unconstitutional. The hon. member is a very astute lawyer. He sat in the House during the time the Civil Service Act was constructed; and so far as the record shows he did not suggest at that time this question of unconstitutionality.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: It was his second year as a member and he was very modest.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
I realize that the hon. gentleman, can, with some degree of honesty, plead modesty. But I notice he made no reference at that time to the important^ matter of unconstitutionality, and although he has sat in the House for a considerable period since I have failed to notice the slightest intimation from him of this problem of unconstitutionality. In fact, I must express the amazement I felt when I ascertained that in 1921 he actually refused to support a motion then before the House asking for the return of the patronage system. There was no suggestion of unconstitutionality at that time, and surely even my hon. friend would not plead modesty at that late date.
There can be no doubt that this question of unconstitutionality sometimes leads to a most profound argument, sometimes to even the shallowest. Whenever we desire to raise any question, I care not whether it be high freight rates in British Columbia or high freight rates in the Maritime provinces, we plead unconstitutionality-some divergence from our confederation pact. But I would suggest that in respect to our civil service legislation such an argument has little merit, and that the only effect-I will not say the designed effect-of my hon. friend will be to-undermine the confidence of the public in the Civil Service Commission.
In the next place, I should like to ask the House who is asking for a change in the Civil Service Act? Who desires a return to
The Civil Service

the patronage system, either unreservedly or qualifiedly? Do the civil servants ask for the abolition of this commission? I think not. In fact, if I judge the situation correctly, that is the veiy thing they do not want. I notice that at a convention of the civil servants in the Customs department held some months ago-and I do not know of any member of the government who displays more enthusiasm for the abolition of the Civil Service Commission than the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau)-they passed this resolution:-
Resolved that this convention of the Dominion Customs and Excise Officers' Association assembled, representing as it does members of the customs and excise service from coast to coast, very strongly resent any attempt to revert to the patronage system, which we feel would be detrimental both as regards the efficiency and the economical administration of the public service, and further that copies of this resolution be forwarded to the Premier, the Hon. Mackenzie King, and the press, urging upon the government in the strongest terms possible the wisdom of giving such matter very careful consideration before allowing the introduction of any legislation which would deprive efficient civil servants the benefits of the merit system as now provided for under the Civil Service Act.
I have no doubt that that expresses to a very large extent the attitude of the Civil Service generally.
Do the public desire a change? Well, I want to read one or two editorials which I think indicate the view of the public on this question, and I would particularly direct the attention of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to an editorial appearing in the Winnipeg Free Press of June 16th last, in which it is stated:-
The defeated candidates have not had this privilege to a sufficient extent, however,-
That is, the privilege of patronage.
-and some of them recently met in Calgary under the chairmanship of Hon. Frank Oliver to frame a formal protest to Premier King according to a circumstantial report in the news columns of the Edmonton Journal. It states-
I take it that that means the Edmonton Journal states:-
It states that seven defeated Liberal candidates attended the meeting and passed a resolution reminding Mr. King that they had requested last January that party and patronage matters in Alberta should be dealt with through the defeated candidates acting on the advice of the Liberal executives or patronage committees, and that he had replied that this, the customary practice, would be adhered to and that "no outside channel will be recognized in dealing with party and patronage matters".

The newspaper report indicates that it was Hon. Frank Oliver, a former member of this House. I was about to quote, Mr. Speaker, portions of an editorial which appeared in the Calgary Albertan, a newspaper not unfriendly to this government. Then, in the second place, the Prime Minister suggests in his address not only a lack of economy but also a lack of efficiency in the operation of this board. He says that if the government were not manacled it could reduce the number of civil servants. How, under these circumstances, a government can complain that the increase in the number of civil servants is due to the Civil Service Commission, is more than I can understand. speechtext:
Now, Mr. Speaker, if what I have already said is not a sufficient indication of economy of the administration of the Civil Service Commission, I would direct the attention of hon. membefs to 4p.m. the report of the commission for the year 1921. I do not know whether a report has been issued for the current year;
I doubt it. On page 6 of this report I find, under the heading of reorganization, these remarks:
At the request of the Deputy Minister of the Department of Militia and Defence, the Commission assigned one of the staff of the Organization branch as a member of a departmental committee on reorganization. This committee's functions were investigational and advisory, and its recommendations subject to the approval of the deputy minister and where necessary, the concurrence of the commission.
The committee has reported on two branches of the department and its recommendations, which have since been put into effect, have resulted in a saving of approximately 120,000 per annum in salaries on the present permanent establishment, and of $18,000 by the release of temporary employees.
It goes on to show how the service in that particular department has been improved, and then says:
A survey of procedure carried on in the commission's own offices had led to a reduction in the clerical staff of twenty-five positions and a consolidation in the methods of handling certain sections of the routine work. This survey is still in progress and it is believed that further reductions in staff and improvements in procedure can be made.
The Civil Service Commission wherever they have been invited to go into a department have saved the public money, and in addition to that they are apparently making a constant effort to save in their own department. That is borne out by the fact that the number of employees in this department,
The Civil Service

according to the estimates, has been reduced I think by six in number.
May I just interject at this point that I do not know a single member of this coinmission; I do not know a single officer of the commission; I have never to my knowledge met a single individual in that department. I therefore speak without any question as to the personnel of the commission.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Who employed these six that were dropped? Does it not show that the commission were experimenting at the public expense in taking these men on?

Not at all. My hon. friend is just arguing in a circle. I Say that it indicates that the Civil Service Commission are consolidating their work, making it more efficient and effecting reductions even in the limited time they have had so far. I wish to direct particular attention to that part of the Civil Service Commission's report dealing with the Printing Bureau to show how the commission is economizing there.
The report says:
The work of reorganization in the Department of Public Printing and Stationery has been continued by an officer of the commission specially detailed for the purpose.
It goes on to indicate the work of reorganization in the bureau and says:
For the first time in the history of the Printing Bureau so far as can be learned, the Auditor General's Report consisting of three large volumes was this year ready to lay on the Table of the House on the day parliament opened.
Further on I find this:
The commission records with pleasure that no difficulty has been experienced in its dealings with the bureau officials, and all appointments, transfers, and lay-offs have taken place without political or other interference, and it is confidently asserted that the Canadian Department of Public Printing and Stationery,, at the present time, compares most favourably with any institution of its kind in America.
Then I would draw particular attention to this statement:
The number presently employed is 732, as compared rvith 1,150 in 1919, a reduction of 428 in staff with an annual pay-roll saving of 1746.000. It is believed a further reduction in staff can be effected after parliament prorogues.
That is the report of the commission, and I ask hon. gentlemen, can we not give to the members of the commission credit at least for having done some good work on behalf of the public service? And I suggest therefore, that if these facts be any evidence the Prime Minister cannot be entirely justified in stating that there is a lack of economy in connection with that particular bureau.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
All I can say is that the address which the Prime Minister gave in the House the other day gives no indication of the details of the manner in which this economy may be effected. I am not suggesting for a moment that out of this system which has developed in the last five years some minor evils may not have developed, but I do deprecate this constant attack on the Civil Service Commission, without, in some way, indicating to the public the confidence which this parliament has or should have in that commission and in the principle involved in that commission. I want to tabulate, if I may be permitted, very shortly, some of the benefits which it seems to me have accrued as a result of the appointment of the Civil Service Commission since May,
I think it was, of 1918. It has given a guarantee that character, physique and mental fitness shall be the means of getting employment in the departments of government, without regard to political belief. It has

The Civil Service
opened opportunities for public employment to the whole public on an equal footing, where merit alone is the only question involved. It has classified the work and it has standardized the salary schedules by the work done and not by the mere question of political influence. It has promoted by efficiency reports the seniority and fitness for positions. It has, as I have suggested already-and I have given some evidence of it-gone a very considerable length indeed, in the matter of creating efficiency in the public service, and, not only that, but minister and members are no longer harassed by personal applications, by interviews and by letters from people who desire some position in the public service. It has largely eliminated the question of politics from the public service. I remember it was reported, in the early stages of the difficulties which subsequently resulted in the American Civil War, that President Lincoln stated that if he had had the opportunity to give his time and attention to the rising troubles in the United- States, instead of having to devote all his time "to the matter of filling the various offices in the States, he probably would have been able to do something to avert that tremendous civil war; and, therefore, I suggest that nobody shpuld be more grateful than the members of the government themselves and the members of this House for the privilege of being released from the difficulties which arise from trying to exercise patronage.
Then, in addition to that, we have no more humiliating-or at least, we should not have any more humiliating-debates in parliament after elections, in regard to political removals. "The dignity of this House, instead of being lowered, as it has been on occasions, has been very much enhanced. Not only that, but elections have, to a very large extent, been purified by the absence now of promises of the spoils of office. The views which I have advanced are in answer to the reasons which have been urged by the Prime Minister for the appointment of a parliamentary committee to go into this matter, and I say perfectly frankly-and I would say it to any government which was in power making a similar proposition-that I fear very much the result if this important matter is committed to a parliamentary committee. I am afraid that, instead of strengthening the hands of the Civil Service Commission, we will find that they are weakened and that patronage will make a further inroad upon our public life.
Now, on the other hand, what can the government do? Is there anything the government can do to make this service more efficient? If I am correct in my statement that the responsibility for the staff rests upon the government, I suggest that they can meet the needs of economy by cutting the staff to the barest necessities. I would suggest that they should ask the Civil Service Commission or its representatives to go into the various departments of government and assist them in putting those departments on an economical and efficient basis. I would suggest also that perhaps the introduction of joint councils, such as is the case, I believe, with England, arbitration courts might assist very materially in securing the confidence and goodwill of the Civil Service themselves. It has been found in England that practically all the suggestions for reform and for greater efficiency in the service come largely from the civil servants themselves. Why not take advantage of that opportunity, get their suggestions and views, and see if, on that basis, something of value cannot be developed. In the next place, I think we should have a permanent superannuation act, and finally I would say that we should secure a report from the Civil Service Commissioners themselves, not a report from two commissioners, not a report from one commissioner, but a report from three commissioners-if they cannot agree, let them give us separate reports,-indicating after a very-careful survey of the situation how, in their opinion, these much desired ends of efficiency and economy can best be secured.
I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the Civil Service Commission themselves, after the experience which they have had, are probably in a better position than even this House to make suggestions of value. They can if necessary traverse this country from one end to the other and make inquiries, not only from the public, not only from the Civil Service, but from every possible source, as to the means by which the purposes of economy can be achieved, and I would suggest that such an investigation as that conducted by that body, should go over the whole question of the Civil Service, the question of subordination, the question of discipline, of organization, of hours, of pay, of appliances, of holidays, pride in the service, esprit de corps, efficiency, retiring allowance, social welfare, and every other factor which will promote in any way economy^ and efficiency.
In conclusion, I want to say that to my mind, there can be no turning back in this matter. I do not believe the people of Canada for a single moment will tolerate any turning back. What parliament must do is to strengthen, to fortify and to consolidate the progress that has already been made in

order to eliminate from the public service the evils of patronage, and in order to make it a service which will not only appeal to young men and young women as in opportunity to give lives of useful service to the public, but will also combine with that the greatest economy and the greatest possible efficiency.

I am entirely in favour of the return to the act of 1908, and of removing the outside service from the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission. In advocating that I do not wish you to understand that I am in favour of returning to patronage, because it is physically impossible to return to a thing that has never ceased to exist, but I am anxious that patronage should be taken from the hands of those who are not responsible to the people and restored to the hands of those who are responsible.
I listened to the speech made by the junior member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) with great interest. He delivered a very serious and instructive speech, and I was amazed when the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mc-Quarrie) referred to him as a joker. I must remind the hon. member for New Westminster that besides a joker there is also a blank card in every pack.
One of the reasons why I am in favour of returning to the act of 1908 is because there has been too much of a tendency, to administer affairs in this country by commissions. We have the Railway Commission, the Purchasing Commission, the Civil Service Commission, and even the Canadian National Railway Company is a commission. I believe that the fMr. Shaw.]
administration of public affairs by commission is detrimental to responsible government. The surest way to get rid of responsibility is to appoint commissions that are not responsible to the people. Under the prevailing system the Civil Service Commissioners in Ottawa can appoint men to different positions all over the country, from the Atlantic coast to British Columbia. How are three gentlemen, living in Ottawa, in a position to know the qualifications of men who make applications for positions in rural constituencies, that are, for example, four hundred miles away from this city? Even the ministers themselves, who are responsible to the people, cannot exercise control over their deputy ministers or their principal clerks. It is a fact that under the Civil Service Commission we have seen principal clerks in departmental offices, and even deputy ministers, criticising the work of the ministers, and there is no possible way of getting rid of them except through the Civil Service Commission. I know what my hon. friends opposite will say in regard to that; they will say that they can be dismissed by an order in council. But who will name the gentlemen to replace them? It will be the Civil Service Commission.

speechtext: Not in the case-

Not in the case of deputy ministers, but it is true in the case of very important clerks. In cases like this-and there are many instances of the same character-how can the minister at the head of a department have efficiency in that department if he has practically no control over his clerks, if even his orders are disobeyed, and his hands virtually tied by the Civil Service Commission?
The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw), in advancing reasons for the maintenance of the Civil Service Commission, stated that the act was a guarantee of character, of merit, without political influence, in the civil service. Surely my hon. friend was not serious when he made that statement. It would be very easy for me to cite a great number of instances where the appointments were made not according to character, not because of merit, but by reason of political influence-not of the present government but political influence in the Civil Service Commission itself. I make this statement with a due sense of the responsibility attaching to it. I can give the House the inside history of a few nominations. We have been told, for example, that when a rural postmaster is to be appointed, the Civil Service Commission despatches an inspector to the constituency where the vacancy has occurred.

The Civil Service
This inspector is supposed to interview the principal residents of the locality, generally the clergyman, the doctor-

speechtext: The lawyer.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: The lawyer sometimes, the mayor, in short the most eminent people of the locality; and, after having interviewed these persons he makes a report to the Civil Service Commission declaring who is the best man to be appointed. Well, Sir, there was a case in my own constituency where such an inspector was sent. It is true he interviewed the mayor; that was on a Tuesday morning. He interviewed the priest in the afternoon. There Was no lawyer in the place. He interviewed the principal merchants there, and then returned to Montreal. Everybody thought he was going to report tc the Civil Service Commission in order that they might make the appointment. But the same night a certain person in the locality took charge of the post office. The inspector did not visit the district to take pointers from the people there who knew the conditions so as to be enabled to make a good appointment, he went there to appoint a postmaster, and the postmaster was on the job the same night. And it happened that he was one of the three electors, amongst 355, who voted against me at the election.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: One of the best arguments brought forward by my hon. friend from Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) was that of economy, but I believe I can show to the House that it would be economy to abolish the Civil Service Commission. subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: That may be true, but we are under a Liberal government. We are not getting all we want, but we are proceeding in the right direction. However, there is still a long distance to go-a hundred and thirty-four employees now against only nine in 1909. My hon. friend will admit that, and he will also admit that there is still a big difference between $12,000 in 1909 and $312,000 last year.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend, but he will surely admit that the Civil Service Act of 1908 only applied to something like 2,000 employees, whereas according to the figures now presented that number has increased to something like 55,000.
Mr. ARCHAMBAULjT : I do admit that, and that is why I want to revert to the act of 1908.
My hon. friend has also said that public opinion is in favour of the maintenance of the Civil Service Commission. I have in my hand an editorial from a paper which cannot be called a Liberal paper-the Montreal Gazette, which in its issue of February 19, has this to say on the subject:-
The act of 1916 was passed with the avowed purpose of eliminating party patronage as exercised in the making of appointments to the Civil Service, the initial mistake being the assumption that patronage is, psr se, an evil, The principle was condemned, in reality, be-

The Civil Service
cause it had been, or was alleged to have been, abused in the making of appointments that were unnecessary and, in the matter of individual fitness, improper. Parliament thereupon did what is so often done in the name of reform; it went to an extreme, and the result is just what always comes of an action of that kind. The law of 1916 set up a system in which the authority of the government was delegated to a commission, and appointments and promotions have since been made in accordance with a scheme of ironclad regulations devised and controlled by the commission, and the so-called merit system has been exemplified in a series of very extraordinary examinations, often upon subjects ridiculously remote from the requirements of the service. The results have not been satisfactory. The efficiency of the service has not been increased nor has its spirit improved, and there is no evidence that economies have been effected as regards the number of the personnel. There is still patronage, but is is exercised, as pointed out by the Prime Minister, by an irresponsible body, instead of by the government and parliament upon whom rests the responsibility for the conduct of the country's affairs. The thing is wrong, is known to be wrong and yet there exists a timorous
reluctance to alter it	Since then, some sporadic
efforts have been made to render the system less objectionable, but what is necessary is a thorough overhauling of the whole machine and the establishment of another order of things, one in which the responsibility of the government will be recognized and restored.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that I have given sufficiently to the House the reasons why I am in favour of the amendment that the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) intended to move. I am informed, however, that one hon. gentleman on this side of the House will take care of that amendment. I am in favour of a return to the law of 1908, taking away the exterior service from the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission. To sum up I may say that my first reason is that of economy; my second reason is that, patronage still exists under this law, but instead of being in responsible hands it is exercised by those who are not accountable to the people; and my third reason is that although neither the government nor hon. members have anything whatsoever to say about appointments to the Civil Service, they are held responsible by the people for all the appointments made and for the fitness of the appointees, a state of things which is absolutely unjust, unfair, and unconstitutional.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if there is one subject upon which we might expect hon. members would come to practical unanimity it is the one now under consideration. Yet we find a very great divergence of opinion, because the subject involves the efficient and economical working of our parliamentary institutions. But because of that very fact we should as business men be able to arrive at a conclusion without, in my judgment bringing any prejudice or partisan feeling into play.
Now, I shall endeavour to present some of the historical aspects of this question. Previous to 1918 there had grown up a body of opinion in the country which felt that the evils of government patronage had assumed very large proportions. I think that opinion was exaggerated. There were, no doubt, some evils, but my impression is that in trying to cure them we brought in fully as many and perhaps more. In 1918 the matter had been receiving very careful consideration in the press and in parliament, and an effort was then made to remedy the alleged evils by an act of parliament. Acts of parliament do not always remedy the evils they are intended to alleviate. It is to be assumed, however, that the late government, who put the act into operation, were in sympathy with its provisions. The commission was appointed by that government and proceeded to work under that act. But the measure was found to be impracticable and unworkable; and I have the best possible proof for that, because the late government brought in a body of experts from Chicago, known as the Arthur Young Company, to assist the Civil Service Commission, and the government and the Civil Service in bringing order out of the chaos which even then existed under the operation of this act. Well, that body of experts failed to bring about workable conditions, and another bunch of experts were brought in from the United States-I refer to the Griffenhagen concern. At very great expense to the country they worked for a considerable length of time, but they also failed; apparently they made confusion worse confounded, and the conditions became very bad. I will not depend upon newspaper reports with regard to those conditions; I will take the statements made by members of the late government or gentlemen supporting them, to show how impracticable the whole thing was. It was stated by a member of the then government on May 2, 1921-the statement will be found on page 2875 of Hansard of that year-that a certain position had been advertised for; that four hundred applications were received for the position, and that the Civil Service Commission were appalled at the number of applications which came in. They could not examine all these applications, and they did not try. They appointed three men in Ottawa, one of them the editor of the Journal, to go over them. When these gentlemen saw the number of applications that had been received they too were appalled at the magnitude of the task. Well, according to a statement of a minister of the Crown in the government of that day, they threw three hundred of these applications into the waste paper basket without looking at them at all; then they made
The Civil Service

a cursory examination of the remainder and recommended a name to the Civil Service Commission for appointment. I assume that their recommendation was acted upon. Now, I ask hon. members of the House, was that an appointment by the Civil Service Commission? Was that an appointment on a business basis? Was that fair to the three hundred persons whose applications were thrown to one side without any consideration at all? Was that an appointment according to merit? It was a minister of the Crown who made that statement.

speechtext: What'minister?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: The member representing Frontenac at that time. I do not know what position he held in the government, but he was a minister of the Crown.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: He was not a minister at that time.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: That was in 1921.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: He was not a minister when he made that statement.	.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Well, he became a minister shortly after.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
On the same day, page 2859 of Hansard, the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) said:
Mr. Speaker, I have never been able to see any merit in the Civil Service Act, because I believe it strikes at the very foundation of responsible government.
I think so, too.
As it has worked out I thihk it might very well have been described as "An Act to Destroy the Discipline of the Civil Service and to Promote Inefficiency."
I will give a statement of another member supporting the late administration, the then member for North Perth. I will not quote his words, but they may be found on page 2280 of Hansard, May 2, 1921, He went on to show that the work the Civil Service Commission had to do was so extensive that they were not attending to it at all, or not attending to it in any proper way. He gave this illustration: A certain position was advertised for, and a certain man sent in his application. Some months passed, and having received no notice in regard to the matter he made inquiry of the commission concerning the paper he had sent in. He received a reply stating that he would have to know the French language before he could be appointed to the position in question. He said, "My application showed that I am familiar with the French language." Apparently the paper had not even been read. He followed the matter up, and later the commis-

sion told him that the position would have to go to a returned soldier. "Why," he said, "my application showed that I was a returned soldier; I went over early in the war and did not come back until after the armistice was signed." Another position became vacant in the post office in Toronto, and a returned soldier who had undergone a double amputation, having had both his legs taken off, applied for the position; it was that of attending the switchboard in the post office. He did not get it; another man was appointed. The position of stamp vendor became vacant, and he applied for that. He was told that that position had been given to another person, and that he had better apply for the position of letter carrier-and that man had both legs off. It may just be possible that the Civil Service Commission has so much work to do that they cannot attend to these things; but in their efforts to control everything they have certainly gone far beyond what I believe was the intention of parliament at the time of the passing of the act of 1918. I have some other cases here, but I do not think I need refer to them.
Some amendments were made to the act in 1921, and the fact that the late government found it advisable to bring in the Spinney Bill to amend the Civil Service Act is the best possible proof that it had come to the decision that the act ought to be amended. I should think that is the best possible proof to convince hon. gentlemen opposite. Then we have the present government stating-and I submit that men in the responsible position of a minister of the Crown when they make a statement in parliament should receive consideration

that they find the system unworkable, impracticable to a very large degree, and expensive. I remember the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) giving a concrete instance last year. He wanted two men for seasonal work and applied to the Civil Service Commission, but before he could get them appointed, the time for doing the work had passed, and it had to remain undone. Is it fair, is it reasonable, is it common sense, that the members of this House and the people of this country should expect efficiency from the government under such conditions? People do not expect it in any other kind of business. If the heads of departments of a large corporation, for instance, told the directors that they simply could not get along properly under their present system of appointments and promotions, what would the directors do? They would certainly allow their managers a very large voice in appointing their clerks and assistants and in making promotions and allotting the work. I do not

The Civil Service
think it is a far-fetched comparison to compare parliament to a business corporation. We, the members of the House, are the directors for the time being, and the members of the government are the managers of the country's business, and we should not in justice look to the managers for proper results unless we give them control in a large measure over their assistants. If their selection and promotion is left to an outside body entirely, we cannot expect good results. I think anybody with an open mind who listened to the speech made by the junior member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) the other night must have come to the conclusion that the Civil Service,Act requires overhauling and amending, or we shall have greater inefficiency and more chaos than we have now.
What should we do under these circumstances? The Prime Minister has made the suggestion that the whole matter be referred to a special committee of the House. Can anybody suggest a better proposition? That proposition was not accepted by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), and the leader of the Progressives (Mr. Forke) withheld his assent; I do not know whether he was entirely opposed to it or not.
But can either of these members or 5 p.m. any other man suggest a better proposition? The hon. leader of the Progressives did suggest an alternative. He stated that if the present government would study this question in the light of the experience they have had since taking office, and would bring down their proposals to the House, so far as he was concerned he was reads' to give them every reasonable consideration. I would say to the hon. member that that is impossible of fulfilment during this session, I think the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) would be the first to agree with me, if he were in his seat at the moment, that during a session of the House members of the government are so busy with the thousand and one things that come before them daily for adjustment that they have not time to give to a question of this kind the consideration it should receive. Furthermore, if the government brought down such proposals to the House, I fear very much whether it would not be considered that there was partisanship and patronage behind the move. Judging by this debate alone, I believe that the government would be charged with having ulterior and sinister motives in bringing down such proposals. That charge could not very well be made against a report by a committee of this House representing all parties. More than that, such a committee could bring before it the members of the
Civil Service Commission, and if these men have been maligned or in any way misrepresented as the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) intimated, if the work they have done is not fully appreciated by this House and the country, what better place and what better opportunity could be given them than to present their case before a special committee of this House? The deputy ministers could also appear before the committee, the chief clerks in departments, and anybody who had useful information to give, and if a committee under those circumstances could not bring in a report that would be useful to the House, I can see no other way of dealing with this question. We must approach it in some way. It is too important to make of it a political party question. Parliament should have even more interest in this question than the government, because as the years pass, governments will come and governments will go, but parliamentary institutions, let us hope, will endure forever, and we, the members of this House,who have far more time on our hands than the ministers have should be quite willing to do our part in trying to solve this difficulty, and solve it fairly.
I do not think any man in this House or out of it wants to bring back any of the evils that existed under the patronage system. I think that is admitted on all sides. But what in the world can the objection be to have a special committee representing all parties in this House taking this matter up, considering it carefully, hearing all the evidence they can get upon it, and bringing in a report and letting the House consider it? I think, upon second consideration, that the member from Brandon (Mr. Forke) will see how reasonable that is and a number of the members on that side of the House would probably take the same view. There is another reason that I want to present to this House and to my Progressive friends particularly. They take pretty advanced views, more advanced views than the rest of us, I think, in regard to the amount of control, management and supervision that governments should give to several matters. For instance, I think they are in favour of government ownership, control and management of the merchant marine. If I am wrong in that I want to be corrected. It must be because they think that these things could be governed more efficiently and capably by, governments than by men who have had years of experience in that line of business. I am quite sure my Progressive friends are in favour of government buying and selling and marketing wheat, and for the
The Civil Service

reason that they must consider that governments are more capable and more efficient than men who have been engaged in that work for many years. Furthermore, I believe that my Progressive friends have strong views that the government should take greater oversight, control and management of the banking institutions of the country than they have hitherto taken, because they have greater faith in the honesty, the integrity and the ability of governments than they have in the men who have managed and are managing the banking institutions of the country, and at the same time some of these men think that the government is not honest enough and not capable enough to appoint its own servants, or its own officials, to look after the business that pertains properly to itself-that the government is able to mind everybody else's business and not able to mind its own. I do not think I am overstating the case. I hold a different opinion. I hold the view that the government should be allowed large control over their own work, and they should be very wary and careful in taking the management or control of a business that is operated by people who have given years of experience to it.
Mr. Speaker, I see no other way of solving this difficulty than by carrying out the suggestion of the Prime Minister, and doing it this session. I agree with the hon. member for West Toronto that the Civil Service Commission strikes at the very foundation of responsible government, and responsible government has been purchased at too high a price in this country to be lightly regarded or lightly discarded.
I have presented the matter to the House as~strongly as I could in favour of the appointment of a committee to inquire into this whole question, and I therefore move:
-that the word "repeal" in the motion now before the House be struck out, and the following substituted therefor-appoint a special committee for the purpose of inquiring into the operation of-
In order that hon. members may appreciate the effect of the amendment, the motion would read in this way, if my amendment were adopted:
That in the opinion of this House, it is advisable to appoint a special committee for the purpose of inquiring into the operation of chapter 12, 8-9 George V, an act respecting the Civil Service of Canada.
My motion is seconded by the hon. gentleman for St. James (Mr. Rinfret).

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
The question is on the
amendment.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
I note
the resolution of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is advisable to repeal chap. 12, 8-9 George V, an act respecting the Civil Service of Canada.
I presume from the wording of this resolution that the intention was to repeal the whole act and do away with the Civil Service Commission. The amendment proposes to refer to a parliamentary committee, for investigation, . the question of the abolition of the Civil Service Commission. In 1918, when we first passed the Civil Service Act, it was thought by members on the government side of the House that we had for all time settled the question of political patronage. It was a question that was mentioned during the election of 1919 and was a part of the platform of the Union government at that time. Then the Union government passed that act for the purpose of carrying out and fulfilling its pledge to the people of Canada. We passed the act with the full assurance that the people of this country were demanding it, and that they wished that political patronage, which had been used by various political parties throughout the history of the country should be abolished. I think it was admitted by all parties on both sides of the House that that system was capable of a great deal of abuse and that it probably had been abused by both political parties. I cannot say that I have had any experience in regard to that myself. So far as' I was aware, there was not much abuse in connection with that system. However, in .the larger centres of the Dominion it is realized that there was a good deal of abuse, and that it would be in the best interests of all concerned, and the Civil Service in particular, that political patronage should be done away with. The act passed at that time placed in the hands of the Civil Service Commission the appointment, under a system of merit, of all members of the Civil Service throughout Canada. In 1908 an act had been passed taking the control of civil servants, particularly in the inside service, from the various departments. The act of 1918 went further and brought in the outside service, placing under the control of the Civil Service Commission something like
50,000	civil servants throughout the Dominion.
I believe that since that time the Civil Service Commission have endeavoured, with all their might, to give the best service possible to the people of this country. They have instituted examinations by which applicants foi positions under the government were given

* The Civil Service
the opportunity of showing, to properly constituted persons who were capable of deciding the matter in the public interest, whether or not they possessed the qualifications necessary to entitle them to admission to the public service and discharge their duties in a manner satisfactory to the public. The Civil Service Commission did, I think, in some instances, institute examinations which possibly at certain times did not result in giving the best results to the people. I think that in some instances, particularly in the outside service, where a simple academic examination takes place, a person may pass that examination and obtain 100 per cent of the marks required, and yet be not possessed of the qualifications that go to make up a good public servant. There are certain qualifications needed in a civil servant that cannot be disclosed by an academic examination, for example the qualities of the man himself-qualities of head and of heart-which enable him to deal with the public in a way which is pleasing to them; and after all it is the personal element in the outside service which exercises a very important influence. But taking it all in all, I certainly think that since that time the Civil Service Commission have given very good returns to the country, and I certainly would not like to see that body abolished now, or any time in the future.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Would not my hon. friend admit that an academic examination may be misleading in all cases?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
That may be true in
certain cases, but I would not feel disposed to admit that it would be a failure' in all, or even the majority, of cases. I think there undoubtedly are certain positions in both the inside and the outside service where an academic examination is absolutely necessary. Without such an examination it would be possible that a person might enter the service who was wholly unfitted for office; I do not think there is any doubt upon that point.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: The hon. gentleman asserts that my suggestion would be possible, would he not admit that it would be probable?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
It might be probable,
in fact I think it has occurred in the past, that persons have been admitted to the public service who lacked the education and the other qualities necessary to render them good public servants.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Do you think it fair that
the Civil Service Commission should delegate the power to an officer-for instance a collector of customs, or some other person-at
a distance to practically make an appointment to an office that was vacant?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
I do not know that the Civil Service Commission delegate authority to such persons to make appointments.
I believe, however, that it is quite within their jurisdiction to ask someone to give 1hem information with regard to the qualifications of certain candidates, and doubtless it is quite proper for them to do so. Such person probably makes a report and the Civil Service Commission might consider his recommendations; I do not think he makes the appointment. I think that under all the circumstances it could not be expected that the Civil Service Commission, sitting in Ottawa, could decide, without some recommendation from the outside, who was the best man to appoint, for example, in the case of a vacancy in the city of Vancouver. I think they must take recommendations from others. Under the act of 1918 they were not permitted to accept recommendations from members of parliament, and I do not know but that might have been a mistake. The resolution before the House simply asks us to abolish the whole Civil Service Act and do away with the Civil Service Commission. The amendment asks that the subject be referred to a parliamentary committee. My impression was that the subject was referred to a parliamentary committee in 1921, when the Spinney Bill was up for consideration, and the committee at that time reported against taking the outside service from the control the Civil Service Commission. The investigation made at that time was fairly exhaustive. All the deputy ministers in the public service were called before the committee and gave evidence and, if I mistake not, with only two exceptions they declared that the Civil Service Commission was in the best interests of the country and that it would be a deplorable thing if the appointment of civil servants, whether in the outside or the inside service, wer taken away from the Civil Service Commission. I believe that two deputy ministers on that occasion did not agree with that view. I think -the Prime Minister, in the speech he made here only a few days ago, stated that at the present time the deputy ministers of the various departments are in accord with the present resolution to do away with the Civil Service Commission, and I was very much surprised to hear that statement. I was wondering whether the present government have changed their views since 1921. Is it possible that the change of government has had something to do with the change of view on the part of the present Prime Minister?

It is apparent from this that the Citizen- which I do not' think is antagonistic to the Prime Minister or his party-also erroneously interpreted my right hon. friend's remarks. Now, with regard to the assertion that the continuance of the Civil Service Commission is not in the interests of economy, I might observe that the various departments of government absolutely control the number of civil servants employed. The Civil Service Commission makes the appointments, but the ministers in the departments can disallow any appointment. They have absolutely in their control the number of civil servants and can reduce that number at any time. It is a mistaken idea that the Civil Service Commission makes the cost of civil government more expensive. The commission has nothing to do with the estimates submitted to the House by the various departments, nor have they anything whatever to do with the number of civil servants that are employed in any department. They make appointments simply at the request of the deputy minister or the minister, and if any appointment is not satisfactory the department can within the space of six months discontinue the service of such appointee and they can reject any one appointed by the Civil Service Commission until they get an appointee who is satisfactory to them. If any department is over-manned, it is entirely within the control of the minister or his deputy to reduce the staff. Consequently if the Civil Service Commission has nothing whatever to do with the cost of administering the various departments or the preparation of their estimates as regards salaries or anything else, it cannot be charged, as is asserted by some hon. members on the
government side, with being in any way responsible for the excessive cost of the Civil Service.
Hon. members will remember that in 1921 there was a re-organization of the Printing Bureau. In that year the government of the day, finding there were too many employees in the bureau, requested the Civil Service Commission to make a reorganization. The commission did so, with the result that the number of employees was reduced from 1,159 to 732, and the more efficient work done by tins smaller staff has effected a saving to the country of some 8746,400 annually. I would suggest to the Prime Minister that he might consider the desirability of requesting the Civil Service Commission to reorganize some of the other departments. I do not pretend that it would be possible to effect a similar economy in every other department, if the minister or his deputy is properly looking after each department and keeping the expense down as low as possible consistent with efficiency; but in view of the excellent results obtained from the reorganization of the Printing Bureau, it is not unreasonable to suppose that equally good results might be obtained in other departments of the Civil Service.
As I stated before, the investigation instituted by the late government in 1921 under the Spinney Bill revealed the fact that the deputy ministers in every department were strongly in favour of the retention of the Civil Service Commission. Probably the right hon. Prime Minister will be able to tell us why it is that there has been such a change of opinion on their part and that they are now in favour of restricting the jurisdiction of the commission to the inside service. It may even be that they claim the commission should be abolished entirely, I do not know.
It has been stated, Mr. Speaker, that the Civil Service Commission is an irresponsible body, accountable neither to the government nor to parliament. I submit that under the Civil Service Act of 190S the commissioners are responsible to the government and to parliament, because although they are appointed for ten years, they can be removed for misconduct by the Governor in Council on an address from the Senate or the House of Commons. If the Civil Service Commission is not giving proper service to the country, if it is not making good appointments to the Civil Service, then it is the duty of the government to take the necessary steps to replace the commissioners by others who may be expected to have a better conception of the obligations of their office. That is one of

the duties which the government owes to the people. For my part, I am making no charge whatever against the Civil Service Commission. Both the commission and its staff have always treated me with the greatest consideration and courtesy. I have not interfered to any extent with appointments in my constituency, because being in a rural district very few appointments come under the commission, and this legislation has not in any way injuriously affected either me or my constituentss.
Last year on the 29th June a reommenda-tion was brought into the House that certain offices under the Crown should be removed from the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission. The recommendation was acted on, and I believe that quite a number of appointments have since been made by the government itself or by its members individually without taking into consideration any recommendation whatever from the commission. That is one step back, so far as the outside service is concerned, to the conditions which prevailed under the act of 1908. I think the present government has made quite a stride in that direction, and it seems to me that the hon. member for Quebec South might have been well satisfied with the promise already made without introducing this drastic resolution.
The amendment moved by the hon. member for King's, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes) referring the resolution back to a committee of the House is only another instance of history repeating itself. Under changed conditions it is possible that such a committee might bring in a different recommendation from that presented by its predecessor. As I look across the floor and find so many hon. members in opposition to the Civil Service Act, I have not any doubt that pressure has been brought to bear upon the Civil Service Commission to get appointments made in accordance with their wishes, and that that pressure is also being brought to bear upon the government, and I have no doubt that pressure will be exerted upon the deputy ministers who may give evidence before such a committee. Consequently it is quite likely that the finding of such a committee might be rather more favourable to withdrawing the outside service from the Civil Service Commission than was the case in 1921. Indeed, it is quite possible that with a large majority of the supporters of the government in opposition to the commission a change will be brought about to suit their wishes. I almost expect to see that happen, although I was pleased to hear the right hon. Prime Minister standing solidly behind the 
Civil Service Act of 1918 as amended in 1919.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to make a long speech on this motion, but I would like to say a few words by way of qualifying the vote that I intend to give on this matter.
Different opinions are entertained as regards Civil Service appointments. Some claim that they would be better looked after by men independent of immediate political influence; others want to establish a distinction between certain positions and to have different classes established in the Civil Service so far as control by the commission is concerned. Still others support the claim that such appointments should remain with the ministers. In all this array of opinions there is one principle which has always appealed to me stronger than any of the euphemisms with which socalled reformers try to clothe their idealistic proposals. It is a principle of plain, simple good sense, namely, that control should rest where responsibility rests. Call it what you wish, patronage or any other name, what we must first ask of ourselves is merely this:
" Who has been entrusted by the people to administer the affairs of this country?" Is it not clear, Mr. Speaker, that we are endowed not only with legislative but also with executive power, that is, the government has executive power and is responsible to the House, which, through its majority, approves or disapproves of the government's actions. It goes without saying that, believing in this principle,
I am against government by commission. At best a commission is only an expediency; it may serve a temporary purpose, but I claim it should not be resorted to as a permanent institution. I do not believe in a commission-

speechtext:
I do not believe in a commission to make purchases for the state, and I do not believe in a commission as a permanent body to appoint functionaries or employees for a responsible government. Not that I revel in patronage, Mr. Speaker; not that I wish to feed on it politically or reap the benefits of it; far from it. Of all the functions that a member of parliament has to exercise, none appeals to me less than the dispensation of patronage. I am a man of study There is nothing I would like more than to lock myself in a library and study the respective merits of proportional representation, or the single tax, or indulge in any other speculation of the mind. But if a poor man, one of the many thousands who have placed their trust in me, knocks at my door, I do not feel that I am right in pursuing the phantasy of my study; I consider I must close my book and open the door.
The Civil Service

Others look at patronage as an evil; I look upon it as a duty-a sad and trying one, yet a duty that our constituents expect us to fulfil. It is all very well to uplift our minds to the serene regions of idealism, but it has appeared |to me that often the revulsion against patronage verges on an unconscious desire for idleness or freedom from a very trying and unsavoury obligation.
When a man requires my help-and may I say that in city ridings at least an elector is' a man known to us only by his residence, his political colour we have no means to ascertain-I do not find that I can say to him: "You have appointed me to look after your welfare, but my hands are tied. What you have to do is to write to a group of commissioners appointed by a government long since gone out of office-it is to them that you must apply." If I am to be held responsible, Mr, Speaker, I claim my share of control.
I do not consider, either, that the present system has shown more efficiency than the old one. The system of examinations is an arbitrary one; it never covers the field that is to be later explored by the appointee, and when it is extended to the more modest functions of the service it becomes a mere farce. Imagine holding an examination for the appointment of a sweeper-a competition of sweepers, with delicate instruments to record the quantity of dust removed, should prove of great interest. And I do not believe that a postman needs to know more about geography than that of his immediate vicinity. I submit that at their best, examinations are a very arbitrary way of making appointments.
I am not ready to admit that this method has done away with patronage, as has been said; not at all. It is merely taking patronage from the hands of responsible ministers and placing it in the hands of life-long appointed, irresponsible commissioners. I believe in going to a minister to discuss a matter of this land. When a member is made a minister he still remains a human being, but when he becomes a commissioner he is involved in a new state of mind that may carry him anywhere, and without pointing to any one in particular I may say that if you wish to develop autocracy in this country you are doing it right along by multiplying the number of commissions composed of irresponsible persons carrying out work that should belong to responsible people.
I need not add that I am not a strong believer in the Civil Service Commission. The only argument advanced in favour of it is that it is able to perform a work that we were

elected to accomplish, but that we are unable to do ourselves. I cannot admit that. If we keep going in that direction we may in the early future appoint another commission to adopt legislation and sit in parliament in our stead, and then the claim of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader), that our indemnity is too high, will have been vindicated.
I am willing to vote for an amendment to submit the whole question to a committee, because I understand that it may be imprudent to put a stop abruptly to a system, however disputable, that has obtained for a number of years. It has been suggested that such a committee has sat in previous years. I submit Mr. Speaker, that this is altogether a new parliament, a parliament that has had no occasion to submit its opinions on this matter, and I believe that this is an argument that should appeal especially to the Progressive group. I strongly hope that parliament will see its way clear to appoint such a committee, and I hope that whatever the results may be, they will be in accordance with this principle, which I consider is of high importance, that control and responsibility should go together. I shall vote for the amendment.
