speechtext:
Permit me.
Mr. Speaker, to crave the indulgence of the House for a very few minutes to make a few remarks on this subject. In the first place, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) for his calm discussion of the subject, for his reasonable, instructive criticism, and for the valuable suggestions he has made with a view to remedying the defects of the service. He, along with other members of this House, traced the history of the Civil Service Commission, noting its growth for the four short years of its existence, and I would like to draw the attention of the House to the character of these four years. They were years ripe with unrest, full of effort to establish returned men, years of return to a normal condition and years of reduction of abnormal staffs which had been increased by war burdens. In the f ice of these difficulties, Sir, one would naturally expect that we would be asked to be patient with the work of the commission, that we would give it time to reach the years of normal condition before the House could be asked to behead an innocent victim; an innocent offender, and, in common with the hon. member for Calgary West, I should like

The Civil Service
to ask now where comes the demand for this decapitation.
The last speaker gave as his reason the objection to government by commission, and yet a very few months ago this government placed under the administration of a commission the affairs of our National Railway. We heard no objection at that time nor have we since to government by commission. I do not criticize the government for this commission, I rather approve of it, because no government, or no cabinet, either in the past or yet to come, can undertake, with any measure of success the work or the administration of these railways. Neither do I believe that any cabinet or government could carry on with any measure of success the Civil Service of this country.
What then is the cause of this effort to decapitate the commission? I think you will rather find it in the words of the last speaker who expressed a desire to retire to his office where he would study the subjects of proportional representation, the single transferable vote, or rep. by pop. But in the midst of his study, in the midst of his dreams, there came a rapping at the door.
Now, Sir, we are all familiar with the work of the elements of nature. Repeated rap-pings can get upon the nerves -of any man or any body of men. Let me state again that repeated rappings can get upon the nerves of any man. or organization of men, and I have no fear but that these rappings have got upon the nerves of the government. If they continue long enough the air, the atmosphere, the attic, the cellar, the empty rooms, and the walls will all be inhabited by spirits and this rapping will continue. On more than one occasion we have heard of the work of the elements of nature. Two years ago our friends, the farmers of Ontario, had experienced the force of the elements of nature. Winds were constantly taking their words from their mouths and translating them into language they were not acquainted with, words they had never spoken. The wind was given as the cause for all this trouble, and so I think this move has been caused by the rappings. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself, no doubt has heard these rappings. There came a rapping from Alberta, and when he went to the door the Hon. Frank Oliver was there. Defeated candidates have been affected by these rappings. The members of the government, the elected members, have become affected by these rappings, and I have no doubt the minister in charge of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment- (Mr. Beland) has heard many rappings from my own constituency. Some of them have taken the form of a rifle or a pistol held at his head, and demands have been made upon him. These are the causes of this move, I am afraid, and the rappings upon the door represent the demands of all the members and their supporters, and now comes this unexpected move to decapitate the innocent commission. _
I would like to pass from these rappings and writings and ask the government to pay attention to the voice of independent people, such as the voice of the hon. member for Calgary West, and in addition I would like to call the attention of the Prime Minister, although he is not in his seat to-night, to his words on page 368 of Hansard, where an independent voice spoke in this country and gave warnings of what was going on, and to draw the attention of the House to the occasion on which this voice was heard. The Prime Minister, in speaking, referred to the letter of Dr. Grant, and said:
This civil service reform movement is supposed to be a reform movement, a moral reform. This is a strange kind of morality, to stir up antagonisms by false representations concerning the government, then claim that such a movement is helping along the cause of morality in this country. I say, Mr. Speaker, that when a principal of a college of young men will lend himself to that kind of false representation with respect to any branch of the public service in this country, the time has come-
And so forth.
These words were spoken with regard to a statement issued by Dr. Grant and I would like to draw the attention of the House this evening to the character of the man who made the statement referred to. There were two very celebrated men produced in this country, who were known by their breadth of vision and by their efforts to upbuild the country as a whole. One was Sir John A. Macdonald, the other was Principal Grant. The latter was a son of Nova Scotia, a province which is noted for the numerous talented men it has given to the public life of Canada, men who have become famous from one end of the Dominion to the other, and I know of none of them more celebrated than Principal Grant. Dr. Grant is the son of the celebrated Prinicipal Grant. Now, one would judge from the remarks of the Prime Minister when he spoke the other day that he was referring to a person unfriendly to his government. Those of us who have been college mates of Dr. Grant well know that he is not unfriendly to this government, that he is imbued with the principles of the Liberal party, and therefore the Prime Minister was not speaking of an opponent but of one of his own strong supporters. I do not think such words should have been spoken of any person who holds
The Civil Service

a position such as that of Dr. Grant. What is the effect of such utterances? It is to deter citizens of this country from expressing any opinion in regard to the public administration. Those of us who have, perhaps, taken some interest in public aflairs, municipally and otherwise, know how often we have gone to the place of nomination on the day fixed and found that there were not sufficient electors present to nominate candidates for the different positions We have had occasion to regret that so few take an interest in the public affairs of Canada, and yet as soon as one man shows his interest in the administration of the government, he is immediately spoken of by the Prime Minister of Canada in the language which I have read from Hansard. I think it is only fair to the gentleman in question that the Prime Minister should withdraw any words derogatory to his character.

MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
I have listened with a great deal of attention to this debate on civil service reform. I have paid considerable attention to what members have said on the government side to see if they could show any reason or advance any sound argument why a committee should be appointed to look into the question. I have no serious objection to the appointment of the committee itself, if it is not a camouflage to try to place the onus of the blame upon this
The Civil Service

parliament as a whole. I cannot myself see why ministers who have been in power now for more than one session, and who have become familiar with the working of the Civil Service and with its evils, if there are any, cannot come forward in a manly way, assuming full responsibility, and say to us, as members representing the people of Canada, that the Civil Service Commission, with its intrigue and other evils, which they believe to exist, is not a workable one and that therefore they would ask for power to remedy those evils. But they have not done that. Not the government, but ordinary members on the government side, simply come to the House and make certain statements that seem to suggest that evil is rampant in the Civil Service, and ask us as a body in this House to vote for the appointment of a committee to investigate those evils; and then in some mysterious way this parliament will endeavour to remedy the same.
Now, the only member I have heard on that side who has brought forward any argument at all to show why the committee should be appointed is the hon. member who has just ' sat down (Mr. Marcil). All the other members who have spoken on the other side, far from saying that they want the committee, express the feeling that lies deep down in their hearts that they wish to have the Civil Service Commission removed altogether. They were not afraid to say so; they were quite frank in the matter. For that reason I am glad to know that there are hon. members on the government side of the House who when they were not in power believed sincerely in the Civil Service Commission. Because I believe that I think the Civil Service is safe.
My hon. friend suggested that public opinion is changing. I want to say to the government that it is on the strength of this theory of things changing that they are able to bring forward these various changes, such as they are doing to-day. The reason why they are not lowering the tariff to a greater extent than they are at the present time is evidently because public opinion, according to them, has changed since they got into power. Someone has said that one of the great blessings of humanity is the fact that we are able to forget promises and disagreeable things. But I am glad to say that there are some hon. members in the House, and some people out of the House, who read and remember, and who now recall that when certain ministers who sit on the government side to-day were in opposition they came out strongly for the Civil Service. And in order to remind the government of certain things that may induce 
them to be consistent, and in the hope that their voice may still be heard and that they may know how to vote, I will read some things that were said some time ago. Speaking in regard to the Spinney Bill which to a large extent was the same as the amendment that is proposed to-day, the Prime Minister on May 2, 1921, is thus reported:
The whole purpose of Civil Service reform was to remove altogether the possibility of ministers acting in a partisan way. If a measure of this kind (the Spinney Bill) is permitted to pass it is setting back in a very real and substantial way the efforts of the past few years in the direction of civil service reform.
That is what the present Prime Minister said on May 2nd, 1921. Now, conditions have not changed materially in regard to the Civil Service; they are changed in regard to the government of the day. As far as the Civil Service is concerned, conditions are much the same as existed when that statement was made. Why then, does the Prime Minister to-day say that it is absolutely necessary for the sake of economy and service that the civil service legislation shall be changed?
But I would also like to quote, if it is permissible, the hon. gentleman who was elected to the first place in this House. The Speaker with all his parliamentary experience and ability expressed himself in these words in answer to a question respecting the Civil Service:
My hon. friend knows that my hair turned grey during that regime. I was between the devil and the deep sea all the time.
He is speaking in reference to political patronage. He proceeds:
It is a new departure in Canada. Let us live up to the promises, aye the sacred pledges made by gentlemen on both sides of the House when through the legislation in this respect adopted two years ago, we declared this country virtuous. I believe in the merit system. This bill is opposed, by the commission, by the independent press of Canada, and generally by public opinion. The Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) stated, when he introduced the bill the other day, that the commission had had an enormous task to perform. That is true, and it is because of the very extent of the task that there may have been some disappointments in the administration of the act. The reclassification in itself was a tremendous task, and although some mistakes were made, we must give the commission credit for having accomplished it. Is there any hon. member on this side or on that side who wishes to revert to that devilish system of political patronage, especially during election time? Let us get free from that system and give the commission an opportunity to exercise its full authority under the protection of parliament. Let that commission administer the act free from all influences. I was not a political friend of Dr. Roche or of M. Jameson when they sat in this House. They were, however, both personal friends, but as a Liberal, dyed-in-the-wool, I have the utmost confidence in the honour of Dr. Roche and Mr. Jameson; I fully trust their integritjr, and parliament should support them and Mr. LaRochelle as well.

The Civil Service
Here then is the statement of the Speaker of the House when as a private member he was revealing unto us the devilish system of patronage, knowing that all the time he was between the devil and the deep sea, and when he looked upon the Civil Service Commission as something that freed him from the octopus that was throwing its tentacles around members of the government. Is it in order to revive this devilish system that we had this exhibition of camouflage this afternoon whereby certain members on the government side while not supporting the amendment stated quite frankly their belief that they should have the responsibility of making certain appointments to the Civil Service, and indeed that the Civil Service Commission should be abolished altogether.
Now, I want to ask this question: Why does the government wish to get rid of the Civil Service Commission? What earthly object is there in doing that?

Under one proposal he would get rid of the commission; that is to say, he would put into the hands of some other people the lower class appointments-he dwelt a greal while upon the lower class positions-although apparently by order in council, passed at the suggestion of the Civil Service Commission, those very classes have been withdrawn from its control. But at any rate he would place one class outside the jurisdiction of the commission, and he referred to the responsibility of making such appointments. Quite a few hon. members have stressed the point of responsibility in the matter, and one hon. gentleman asked the hon. Minister of Finance whether he would continue the present system if he were in a great business.
Well, there is this to be considered when you are dealing with a great business. As a usual thing the proprietor has been born into the business, he knows all about it from A to Z; but even then in some instances he is not qualified to judge who are the best men to be appointed to certain positions, and so he delegates this duty to one of his managers who is peculiarly qualified to undertake it. I can readily understand that where a new government comes into power every few years it is almost impossible for a minister to acquire such an intimate knowledge of every position in his department as would enable him to select the right man for any vacancy that might occur. For that very reason it would seem to me to be far better to place such appointments in the hands of an independent commission. Why, one hon. member answered the question not very long ago. I do not believe in political patronage. It has been tried in many countries of the world, and it has been found wanting everywhere.
A man who is enlightened; one of the men who has recently seen light on the Liberal

side, who has made an exhaustive study of the democracies of the world, says that if you revert to any condition of patronage, you are making a retrograde movement. That is where we stand to-day. No country in the world than can claim the name of democracy would go back to the patronage system that we have heard so much about this afternoon. What seems to be the matter with the Civil Service in the minds of some hon. members is that those hon. members have failed to get the people appointed whom they wanted to get appointed.
Now, one hon. member asked certain questions, and I would like to answer them. It was the hon. member who attempted to pour oil on the troubled waters; I think it was the hon. member for King's, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes).

All right; I am not speaking of any particular government; I am referring to governments and businesses in general. We believe so far as the Civil Service is concerned that its efficiency can best be maintained by an entire absence of political interference. Give them a free hand; let us have competitive results in regard to these things.
Before I close I wish to refer to the rest of the statements that I have scanned as made by members of the present government. The hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Murphy) must

The Civil Service

have known what he was talking about when on April 12, 1918, he said:
I walked up the street feeling for the first time in about three years I was a free man.
It is a glorious thing to be free. The junior member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) spoke in this debate some time ago about all the volumes that were issued as a result of the classification and the volume of correspondence that passed between the government and the Civil Service Commission. I wonder how much correspondence each minister would have if the patronage system came back to-morrow and the ministers had to answer every applicant for a position in the Civil Service. They would have far more correspondence to answer than they have now. The Postmaster General (Mr. Murphy) says:
The feeling was due to the fact that I realized I was free of the curse of patronage. It is because I see in the bill which has been introduced (the Spinney Bill to restore patronage) the possibility of returning to the conditions which I have eluded that I am opposed to its adoption by this House.
Patronage is such a curse that my continual wonder has been that men on both sides of politics would put up with it for the length of time that it has endured.
Of course, hon. members claim that .they do not wish to have the patronage system come back, and I only hope that their expressions are a true criterion of their real wishes, but in listening to this debate I have failed to hear one member on the opposite side of the House deduce a single argument in favour of the commission. I did hear a great deal along this line: You have given us responsibility, now give us the power; let us work out the administration and select the men, as is our right, and so forth. If the government can show by argument that the appointment of a committee is for the purpose of remedying the alleged evils in the service and removing for all time the atmosphere of suspicion that seems to overhang the dealings of the commission, I am willing to support the motion; but if it is
9 p.m. simply to camouflage the real issue and lay the blame on parliament for the condition that they would bring about, I must protest and vote against it. So far the arguments are lacking in its favour.
Mr. H. A. FORTIER (Labelle) Translation) :	Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of maintaining the Civil Service Commission and I wish it to be so understood. In the course of this debate, I heard, on more than one occasion, statements made by members sitting on your left, Sir, in regard to the stand taken by those who support the government.

According to these utterances, it would seem that we have no faith whatever in the Civil Service Commission and that we would be very willing to abolish it. I wish to state emphatically that I am in favour of retaining the Civil Service Commission.
I think this commission plays a most important part in our administration; therefore, our duty is, not only to uphold it, and, if necessary to amend the act that governs it, but also to co-operate with it in the most loyal and thorough manner.
The reasons set forth against this commission only bear out the more, to my mind, that it should exist. Some of these inferences would tend to discredit the commission by bringing out concrete cases of blundering attributed to it. To my view, Sir, such arguments should convince us the more that if we have an institution that may have erred- and this is somewhat the fate of all human institutions-we should endeavour to amend the act by which it is governed so as to prevent any further wrongs. In other words, if this institution is sound, we should not destroy it, but it behooves us as legislators to do all in our power to enable it to sail clear of such reefs.
This commission is absolutely necessary for the administration of public affairs. It is also necessary when choosing civil servants who are indispensable to the country. During the first years of Confederation, we tolerated what was known as excessive patronage. However, about fifteen years ago, Canada wisely decided, following in the footsteps of other countries, that the time had come to create a Civil Service Commission. The latter was therefore instituted, much to the country's benefit.
Broadly viewed, the commission's aim is to make known the various openings in the Civil Service, also to decide what qualifications should possess those who enter the service. Again I state, that the Civil Service Commission Act, as amended, is to-day indispensable. I do not say that it is perfect, because all institutions after a number of years of trial, necessarily need reforms to keep up with the times. Such changes are certainly needed in order that the carrying out of it; duties be made more effective and to give to the numerous civil servants, in the Capital, in the neighbouring town, in fact all over the country, the greater feeling of security possible, and, so that those who, in the future, enter the service be judiciously chosen. The work accomplished, after all, is a useful one. Do not the civil servants, of this capital and the town opposite, make up one of the most important sections of the community? Do

The Civil Service
they not belong to a select and privileged class? Amongst them are to be found men of letters, others versed in art or science, it can be said that they are a chosen lot and trusted servants of the State. These employees certainly deserve our praise for the devotion to duty in their various occupations, and as a public man, I deem it my duty to acknowledge this class of civil servants who spare no effort in the interest of our country.
I am not willing to admit that the resolution moved by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) has for effect to destroy confidence in the Civil Service Commission. In the words of the mover and those who supported his motion I find nothing of a nature to bring discredit on the commission. It certainly deserves no blame. A very great task has been confided to them, an enormous undertaking. One little realizes the work that the Civil Service Commissioners and the staff entrusted with the carrying out of this act, are called -upon to perform. This commission certainly deserves praise and on that score I state that I have faith in that body, and, the work which it has accomplished has been for the welfare of the Dominion.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if employees are necessary to the State, it does not follow that all roads must lead to officialdom so that the youth of our country, the flower of the nation, should therein find a safe harbour. I know there are higher, more attractive and more independent callings than those attainable in the public service.
Far be it from me to appeal to the young men of our country and induce them to enter the service. I would rather beg of them to seek more independent, more remunerative positions in which they would be called upon to play a more important part for the welfare of the country. I would rather ask the young men to devote their energies towards the liberal professions, commerce or industry and seek to better serve their country in these broad walks which will be a greater source of happiness than the Civil Service can offer them.
I endorse the amendment moved by the hon. member for King's (Mr. Hughes). I am in favour of this parliamentary committee that should be named to further inquire into the working of this act, so as to avoid the mistakes referred to by the hon. members who preceded me in this debate. I am in favour of appointing this committee so as to amend the act, to make more efficient, if possible, the staff of the commission and to give it the necessary backing in order that the application of this act should become more and more effective. I am again in favour of
appointing this committee, so that the civil servants may have the opportunity to appear before it, make known their aims, claim their rights and expose the difficulties in their path. I< am in favour of appointing this committee so that justice may be done to that numerous class of civil employees who underwent hardships during these last years, at the hands of foreign commissioners appointed by the previous government, to inquire into the administration of the Civil Service Act and who were responsible for hundreds of efficient employees being dismissed without any cause. I want these employees to appear before this committee and explain why, following on the shameful inquiries of Young and Griffenhagen, they were dismissed from the service; I want them to state their case before this committee. After having risen to enviable positions in various departments, many amongst them have become artisans. They had devoted the best of their life to their country and after making a career of the Civil Service, they were dismissed without warning or cause. Perhaps they are at present undergoing hardships in consequence of these shameful inquiries. This committee will afford them the opportunity of making known the wrongs from which they suffered. I have faith again in this committee because it will be a means for the civil servants to establish their claims, for instance, in regard to the bonus, so that it be included in their regular salary and also to revise the scale of salaries. I believe the appointing of this parliamentary committee is certainly justified for the reasons already mentioned by hon. members and those I have put forth. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I shall support the amendment moved by the hon. member for King's (Mr. Hughes) and I will vote against the motion of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) who is opposed to the Civil Service Commission.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
I feel that it is my duty to say a word in regard to this matter. I think that the amendments to the Civil Service Commission should be looked at in a reasonable way, if they are of the class of amendments that are needed. I am not acquainted with the conditions well enough to judge of that. From what I hear, I am convinced, at least, that some amendments could be made that would make the Civil Service more satisfactory and give the government a privilege that I believe they do not now possess. I have had rather an active life. Some people say that I have succeeded fairly well. However, I am not going to boast about that at all, but I have been able all my life, with all the business
The Civil Service

that I have ever handled, to say who would take a responsibility that it was impossible for me to take, when it was more than I could handle. If a minister in the government needs a reliable helper, and we hold that minister responsible for that helper, I believe he should have a chance to say who that helper should be. That is my conviction and at the same time, I am in favour of the Civil Service Commission. I believe that there is work that they could do and should do better than aflyone else. I see no harm in appointing a committee, if that committee is fairly chosen, to go into this matter and present a report to this House.
I warn the government, however, that I am not willing to go an unlimited distance in this matter, and I am not willing for the ministers to have more authority than they should have. I am not in a position to say how much more authority they should have than they possess to-day. I would like to hear the report from that committee. If the committee, in my judgment, goes too far, I will vote against their report. I do not wish to look at this matter from any partisan or prejudiced standpoint. I expect the government to be fair and square, and do as they agree to do. Let them appoint that committee as fairly as they can, and see that all parties are represented. Let the committee go into the matter, and when that report comes to the House, we will have something to work on. I believe that my quarter of the House, or my third of the House, as you might say, is going to be divided on the question. I am stating what I conscientiously believe, I am going to stand by it, and I am going to vote for the committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. P. GRAHAM (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
While in favour of retaining the Civil Service Commission, being one of the men who were responsible for its appointment, I desire to give one reason why I feel, in the first place, that there are some difficulties in the way as the matter stands at present. It is not the fault of the commission, but the fault of the law. I have had the unpleasant experience during the past fourteen months of seeing more than a thousand employees in the Department of Defence retired, not on account of inefficiency, but on account of receding work. These men and women are absolutely efficient, some of them having had five or ten years' experience in the very work of the department. Under the present law, what is their position? They cannot be appointed to any other department, although they possess all the qualifications, except that

they have not passed the examination. Today, every department, I suppose-well several departments at any rate-have advertised for clerks and stenographers, and young men and young women are coming in from all parts of Canada without any experience to accept those positions, while there are thousands of efficient clerks walking the streets of Ottawa, who cannot be appointed.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Those are temporary
employees?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Temporary employees in name; some of them have been there as long as ten years. It may be asked, why were they not blanketed in, that is to say, why were they not made permanent en bloc? Well, in the Department of Defence they could not be made permanent for they were going instead of coming. There was not work for them to do, consequently they could not be blanketed in without any reason. There is something wronf with the act there. Now you say, why not bring an amendment? Well, that amendment might prove impossible in some quarters. I am in favour of the Civil Service Commission being retained, but I do believe that if we had a committee fairly selected from different parts of the House, and just such cases as I have cited placed before them, and if we heard the commission and every person interested, we might find several ways in which the law could be amended without creating any difficulty with the commission and in the final result the operations of the commission would be really strengthened rather than weakened.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot help but express my admiration of the ingenuity of the Minister of Defence in the presentation he has just made. I have been waiting throughout the length of two days to hear some suggestion as to what amendment really was in the mind of the government that required this committee of the House to look into or to draught. I heard none, save attacks on the whole principle of the Civil Service Act, until the minister arose. He, however, has found one now.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: There are others. I have just given examples.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
He says there are temporary employees for example in the Department of Defence and they cannot be transferred to other departments. They are not needed in the Defence department, they are temporary within the meaning, of course, of the Civil Service Act, and some of them

The Civil Service
may have been there for years. They are not needed there, and new ones are required in other departments and these do not get the preference under the law that they ought to get. That is what I understand his argument to be. The Civil Service Commission, of course, can appoint them just as they can appoint anyone else, subject of course to the priority of the returned soldier's claim. The Civil Service Commission can appoint them but there ought to be some preference given them.
. Mr. GRAHAM: How can it appoint them to permanent positions without passing an examination?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Certainly, why should they go without passing an examination?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: That is one of the difficulties.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
If the government thinks they should go without passing an examination there is no amendment in the world easier draughted than that. Surely the government does not want a committee of the House to draught an amendment to enable temporary employees to be transferred without an examination. I question very much the wisdom of it; I question very much the fairness of it; I question very much if this House would pass it. All these things have been considered and reviewed a dozen times. But is what the Minister of Defence has mentioned the real object of this committee? Is there anybody in this House so innocent as to dream that anything of that nature is the object of the committee at all? If there is, then he has not read the speech of the Prime Minister, he has not read any of the speeches delivered up to the deliverance of the Minister of Defence to-night. You cannot read any such object as that into any other speech delivered yet.
Now this comes before the House in very attractive form-I mean the amendment of the hon. member for King's, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes). All the amendment asks for is a committee to look into this Civil Service Act and see if something cannot be done to make things better. Nothing could appear more innocent than that. One would wonder how anybody could object to it.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Oh! "Hear, hear," says
the hon. member for Brome. Does he remember his own speech against the same thing two years ago? Now he cannot understand why anybody should object. Two years have altered his attitude entirely. Two years ago
there was a motion for a committee, and the reasons for it were frankly given from the first. They were not delayed for two days, debate taking place in the meantime on something else altogether, and then some technical suggestions made by a minister. No, after the working of the act for three years the government came before parliament and submitted, that in its opinion there were certain classes of appointments-and suggestions were made as to what they would be-that would be better handled outside of the act. First of all, that there were very minor appointments, certain appointments involving fees and no salary, appointments of labourers and the like; and then there were certain other appointments as respects which the machinery of the act was not adapted; for example the appointment of highly skilled technical men. As to the one class the government, while not naming any series of positions, suggested that a committee consider what in the public interest, might go in that schedule, and as to the second what might go there-the second being distinguished from the first by the provision that the imprimatur of the commission should be placed upon the choice of the responsible minister, both to be extremely limited in their application.
The government did not come to parliament and say "We want the power where we have the responsibility;" we did not come to parliament and present one argument after the other against the very existence of the cjominission itself as this government has done against every useful purpose any commission could serve. No, we came to .parliament and said: "We intend to abide by that act and its principle right through;" that the commission could make appointments; except as respects certain classes which we asked the committee to consider. We asked the committee to consider if there were not certain minor classes that ought to be taken out all together, and we asked the committee to consider as well if there were not certain others that ought to come out but be subject to the commission only to the extent of having to secure the commission's approval. We were resisted in this House, resisted by every hon. gentleman who sits opposite to me, who was here then-resisted to the extent that the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) rose and moved the six months' hoist. They would not consent to a committee of inquiry at that time into these definite suggestions, although the government stated that not only should the principle of the abolition of patronage be maintained but the powers of the
The Civil Service

commission should be retained intact as to everything save those suggestions, We simply asked that these suggestions be submitted to a committee.
Now, does the Minister of Defence's speech really expose the position the present government is in in regard to this amendment? Is there anyone so innocent as to think it does? The government came before this House and, by the speech of the Prime Minister intimated that while they did not want the commission abolished, they wanted to be armed with power to appoint whom they wished. Such was the speech of the Prime Minister. I have that speech here. If anyone can read any other meaning into those words, to be found on page 364 of Hansard I would be very glad to hear from him. Just previously, the Prime Minister said that while he could not agree with the motion he "would like to associate himself with the mover of the resolution in much that he said about the importance of maintaining ministerial responsibility, and having government by a responsible ministry and not irresponsible authority." On the next page, 363, he says:
And the government finds itself-I speak now from the knowledge of the difficulties with which the ministers of the different departments have to contend-the government finds itself continually in the position of being obliged to endeavour to carry on the work of the [DOT] country with clerks who are sent to the government by the Civil Service Commission, but who do not possess the qualifications which if the minister himself were free to make the appointment, he would see were possessed by whoever was appointed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: That is quite right; the Prime* Minister says "hear, hear", endorsing his statement advocating that the ministers be free to make appointments, and asserting that when they are they will make better appointments than the Civil Service Commission makes and obtain more qualified persons.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: In certain cases, yes.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
No, the Prime Minister did not at all say ."in certain cases". He made his statement as a general principle. He says he knows the difficulties ministers have to face when they are compelled to canyon the work of the country -with clerks sent to the government by the commission who do not possess the qualifications which, if ministers were free to make the appointments themselves, they would see' that the appointees possessed. In a word, the government wants the right to appoint clerks. Now,
I ask:-if you take clerks away from the commission, whom would you leave for the commission to appoint?
I Mr. Meighen.]

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: May I answer my right hon. friend by asking him a question? When he established the Income Tax branch why did he not place it under the Civil Service Commission?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: For the simple reason that the employees, when they were appointed, were intended to be temporary. Does the Prime Minister want the whole service placed on the same basis as the employees and clerks of the Income Tax branch? If he does, then he wants to extrail the very heart of the Civil Service Act. In the thoughtlessness of the moment the real purpose of the government came out. What has the *Prime Minister in mind? Is it the putting of the whole service in the position of the Income Tax branch?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Not at all.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Then what was the significance of the question? Here in this speech he appeals to the House for authority to appoint clerks, and asserts to parliament that if the government gets that authority better clerks will be appointed than those who are sent to the departments by the Civil Service Commission. But that is not all, nor is it the worst. I know that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Graham) will marvel at the contrast between the virility of this suggestion and the technicality of his own. At page 364 the Prime Minister says:
May I assert, speaking of patronage, that patronagt cannot be abolished by statute. It is impossible to make appointments to the public service unless they are made by some body. The Civil Service Commission as constituted to-day is a body of three or four men. Hundreds of appointments-yes, thousands of appointments-have to be made to the public service. Those who favour appointment by commission must remember that these gentlemen have the determining as to who is to fill particular positions. They have patronage as long as they have to make appointments. But while they have the patronage they are responsible to no one. The government is without patronage, as matters stand at the present time, but is held responsible for appointments with which it has nothing whatever to do. That is not in the interests of the public service.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: The Prime Minister says "hear, hear". He declares in those remarks that it is not in the interests of the public service that the Civil Service Commission should have power to make appointments, and that while they have patronage they are responsible to no one. This he declares, is not in the interest of public service; and yet he asserts that he does not want a return to patronage! No. wonder the Prime Minister sits perplexed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Does my right hon. friend want me to interrupt him?

The Civil Service

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: I do, if he thinks I am not stating the facts.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
I would ask
the right hon. gentleman what about the ten thousand positions so-called, which the commission itself asked to have taken from its jurisdiction? That is a return to patronage [DOT] at the request of the commission.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT

I did not say

meaning of the words I have quoted?

speechtext:
I said that

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
The Prime Minister did
not say that at all. He said in the language I have quoted that he is opposed to the principle of the commission appointing men, with whose choice the government has nothing to do, but for whose work it is held responsible.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: My right hon. friend attributes the word "principle" to me. I would ask him to find that word in any utterance of mine on this subject.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Well. The Prime Minister said he was opposed to the -practice, and I thought he would be opposed to the principle. I will read again what he says:
May I assert, speaking of patronage, that patronage cannot be abolished by statute. It is impossible to make appointments for the public service unless they are made by some body. The Civil Service Commission as constituted to-day is a body of three or four men. Hundreds of appointments-yes, thousands of appoiritments-have to be made to the public service. Those who favour appointment by commission-
In the following sentence he points out *what is wrong.
-must remember that these gentlemen have the determining as to who is to fill particular positions. They have patronage as long as they have to make appointments. But while they have the patronage they are responsible to no one. The government is without patronage, as matters stand at the present time, but is held responsible for appointments with which it has nothing whatever to do. That is not in the interests of the public service.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Now, I wait for another interruption. If the English language can state antagonism to commission appointment in clearer words than these, then it is beyond my power to find them. It is not in the interests of the public service, he says, that the commission should appoint men for whose work the
government is to be responsible. The moment you come to that stage you are against the commission altogether; or at least, if you are not against the commission, you want a commission that is robbed of all effective power, a commission that is colourless and worthless, a commission that is a mere mummy without any power of appointment. The Prime Minister says he wants a commission-is it to be a commission of that kind? He declares that he is opposed to the power of appointment to the Civil Service resting in the commission and not in the government. But the Prime Minister did not even stop there. He went on to say this:
I think some commission or other body should have the power to see that the members of the Civil Service are duly qualified for their positions before being appointed to them, and that those who are already in the service should secure promotion and salaries in accordance with merit.
I will give the House the significance of this extract in a moment. He continues:
But I do say, Mr. Speaker, if we are to have merit recognised and the measure of justice which we should have for the service, if we are to have that economy and efficiency in the public service which we should have, we shall have to get back to where the government has a larger measure of responsibility for how the public service is carried on where it will have some substantial authority and will not be manacled and, shackled by regulations and rules of a body that is responsible to no one but itself, and that in many cases makes appointments not by itself, but as can be shown if the commission is brought before a .committee of this House, by its own appointees who conduct examinations and make recommendations.
There, again, is an appeal to the House to have the government endowed with power of appointment, not " manacled and shackled " by any body responsible only to itself. I have quoted in three distinct passages from the Prime Minister, the declaration of his belief that the government, in the matter of appointments, should not be shackled by a commission such as he describes, responsible only to itself, and that the government would appoint better men if it had the power under the act to make those appointments. Now, I want to ask again if language could be found that declares more emphatically against the whole principle of the Civil Service Act? I have quoted only from the Prime Minister. But he has been followed by other members on his side who in speech after speech, from that of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) to that of the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), uttered not a single sentence consistent with the retention of the very essence of the Civil Service Act at all.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
If the right hon. gentleman will allow me a question? Would not he

The Civil Service
and the House be in a better position to give a judgment in this matter after having heard the evidence?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: I have heard the evidence. I have heard some witnesses in this debate, and I do not think that witnesses who are imbued with the idea that seems to be behind this amendment will do much to throw any additional light upon the subject. It is all a question-and this House might just as well decide it now-whether we are going to retain a virile Civil Service Commission on its present principle or not. The hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) nods assent. He is perfectly honest and frank about it. Now, that is what we are deciding.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
If the right hon. gentleman will allow me:	When he states that
I am in favour of the retention of a virile Civil Service Commission, he is right. But I say that at present that situation does not exist.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Well, the hon. gentleman nodded assent when I said that what we really had to decide was whether we would retain a virile Civil Service Commission or [DOT]not. He may be quite ready to maintain a virile Civil Service Commission in the physical sense. But what they would have to do, if what he enunciated in his speech becomes law, is a mystery to me. They might have to put their stamp of approval -on some man selected by the government-and I fancy that is what he has in his mind-but to reach that stage is to go back ten years and wipe out ten years of civil service reform. Certain sentences of the Prime Minister's are consistent with that idea too, notably one I quoted but did not comment on a few minutes ago. If such an idea is in the Prime Minister's mind, then he purposes to abolish the reforms- of ten years, he wants to make the Civil Service Commission merely a commission to pass upon the qualifications of appointees of the government-possibly before they are appointed. But I want to warn this House that there is all the difference in the world between giving the government power of appointment subject to the imprimatur of the commission, and giving the commission power of appointment subject to the acceptance or rejection of the government. Therein is all the difference between the act of 1908 and the act of 1918. Evidently what the government has in mind, if the sentence about retaining a commission quoted from the Prime Minister's speech is any indication, and if the interruption of 
the hon. member for Ottarva has any significance, is to reduce the Civil Service Commission to the dimensions or rather to the impotence of the old commission under the 1908 act.
They want to put the power of appointment in the government. That is what the Prime Minister says. They want to do so,. he says, because it is in the interests of the public service. He has made such assertion in his speech, and he cannot escape from his words. If the power of appointment is to be in the government, what is the commission going to have to do beyond what the old commission under the 1908 act had to do? Therefore the question is whether we are ready to go back to the patronage conditions of the 1908 legislation. That is what we must decide on this amendment.
I want to add a word or two more on this question of the Civil Service Commission itself. The words have been loosely used in this debate that the commission is an "irresponsible body." It is not an "irresponsible" body to begin with. The commission, it is true, is not responsible to the government, and is not removable by the government. If you make it so responsible then you merely make it the instrument of the administration, you take it entirely out of the category of a judicial body and make it merely an appointive body-simply an instrument of the government of the day. But the commission is responsible to parliament. Under the terms of the legislation it is answerable to this House, and any member of this commission may be removed on an address of this and the upper House. The standing of the commission in its relation to parliament is similar to that of the Railway Commission, and unless you make it so you have nothing but a camouflage-you might just as well repeal the Civil Service Act altogether. Unless you put the commission in such position you have the government of the day able to exercise patronage to its heart's content.
Now, the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Warner) in the course of his address remarked that a man responsible for the conduct of a business-he meant a private business-had the right, and could not succeed unless he exercised the right, of selecting his own employees, and the hon. gentleman intimated that he favoured such a practice in the business of government. He added that he wanted the Civil Service Commission retained. I am not able to see just what he wants it retained for. If his first principle is embodied in the report of this proposed committee he will never have anything to vote against,

The Civil Service
because it cannot go any further than his own conception that is to put the power of appointment in the government. He argued though that because the head of a private business should have such a right, it is better that the government should have it too. I am afraid the hon. member has not reviewed the history of appointments by governments in this or any other democratic country. The relationship of a government to the affairs of a country differ from the relationship of a man to his private business. A government, of course, is responsible, and the government's duty is to conduct the affairs of the nation as it would conduct its private affairs; but a government, no matter to what party it may belong, is subject to influences, arising from the fact that it must submit itself periodically to the electorate, that to that end it must maintain an organization. Because a government is subject to these influences, unknown in private affairs, it has been deemed wise in almost every country in the world to remove from the control of government for the sake of the government itself as well as of the country this power of appointment of the officers and servants of the State. Why, this is done all through the affairs of this and other countries. It is only lately that it has been applied to the ordinary departmental clerks and the like in the inside and the outside service. But just as democratic government has evolved it has been applied in one sphere and another-in the judicial sphere, afterwards in quasi-judicial spheres as regards our railway telegraph controversies, and then in the matter of the management of the National Railways themselves-I only mention these three-also in the matter of appointments to the Civil Service. It is merely a matter of development, of placing a certain portion of what formerly was the function of government in a position where it can be more efficiently performed in the interests of the state as a whole. Consequently words which may argue well as respects a private business, argue not at all as respects a government; if such were not true we would never have had any Civil Service Act, not even the act of 1908, never the act of 1918. Therefore, I think sufficient attention has not been given by the hon. member to the history of this subject. This House and the country have decided that the influence of patronage-
