subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: No, no.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
They have so talked even to-night.
Now, let us come to what was done under the amendment of two years ago. The amendment simply put it in the power of the Civil Service Commission to make a recommendation to the government that certain classes should be taken away from the operation of the act, and the commission was empowered to make its recommendations, either because it believed that the appointment of that class by the commission was impracticable, or because it regarded such jurisdiction as not in the public interest. These latter words were inserted in order to widen the powers of the commission in the making of their recommendations. Previous to this amendment the commission had power to recommend that any class be taken out if it considered the appointment of members of that class by the commission impracticable.
The Civil Service

Now, following the amendment, classes of a very narrow range, not amounting to any appreciable number, were taken out under the late government on the recommendation of the commission, the government approving of that recommendation by order in council. And the government that approves takes the responsibility ; it cannot hide behind the skirts of a commission. I want to impress that on the Prime Minister. The idea he sought to drive into the minds of hon. members was this: " Oh, we did not take anybody out from the operation of the act; it was the commission." The commission has the power of recommendation, but the power of recommendation does not reduce the responsibility of the government by one iota; the government is responsible for taking every one of these ten thousand men out of the operation of the act. The government can say, " We exercised that responsibility because we had a recommendation; this was the factor causing us to do it." That is all right; that argument is quite reasonable. But the government is responsible for every class and every man that comes out of the operation of the act; for this whole ten thousand the government is responsible. We were responsible for those we approved of-and narrow indeed, almost negligible, was the range of those who were taken out by the late government. As showing that the government of which I was the head had no intention of invading the principle or the operation of the act to any appreciable extent, I would point to the very narrow range of cases that we took the responsibility of taking out while we were in power. Now, this government comes into office and in the month of June, 10,000 are swung away from the operation of the act. Is it any wonder that apprehension surges through the country? Is it any wonder that people come to think that there will probably be further exemptions? Is it any wonder that they think that with twenty per cent of the service gone back to patronage there is danger of more going back as well?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: The right hon. leader of the Opposition mentions 10,000 exemptions. Does he infer that these were taken away under the present administration or under the late administration?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: They were taken away under the present administration.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
May I refer the right
hon. gentleman to the order in council of 21st September, 1921, wherein 'it is stated that all labourers, labour foremen, assistant labour foreman and charwomen are exempted from the operation of the statute?
[Mr. Meighea 1

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
If they are, I do not
know why charwomen are taken out twice, for they appear in this order.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
When that order was
passed the Civil Service Commission simply named in general terms these four classes, and it was not to operate outside the city of Ottawa. But when the order in council of the 29th of June of last year was passed, the Civil Service Commission proceeded to catalogue the positions that came under the category of labourer, labour foreman, assistant labour foreman and charwomen, and extended that to the city of Ottawa. Those
10,000	positions were taken away from the operation of the statute by the late administration, and only those that remained in the city of Ottawa came under the operation of the order of 1922.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: I do not know whether the hon. member merely wants to make a second speech or not, but what he says does not in the slightest degree detract from my argument. I used the figure 10,000 in my speech the other night. Those figures had been used by Dr. Grant. I asked the Prime Minister if he objected; if they were not right-because I did not know whether they were or not-as relating to the number of persons exempted under the order in council of the 29th of June. The Prime Minister said he would not say that the figures were not right; consequently I have a right to assume that there were 10,000 taken away by that order in council.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Is the right hon. gentleman prepared to dispute my statement?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: I do not know what effect the statement has that is of any importance. He says there were some charwomen taken out under the order in council.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
might possibly give the one who has the floor the right to answer his own question. There were some charwomen, as I understood it, taken out by the order in council of September, 1921, but not all the charwomen; the rest were taken out by the order of the *29th of June. I am not in a position to dispute my hon. friend's authority as to when the charwomen came out, but I know they are mentioned in this order.
This order is an order of vast extent. For the most part I quite agree that it covers minor appointments, but there are important appointments included in it. I do not wish to criticize the Civil Service Commission for making the' recommendation, J say this.

The Civil Service
though: a recommendation that takes out garage men, quarrymen, barbers, blacksmiths, boilermakers, boommasters, cabinetmakers, carpenters, ship construction carpenters, caulkers, coopers, coppersmiths, derrickmen, divers, dynamo tenders, electricians, linemen, and all the rest on this list-there are two or three pages; a recommendation that takes those out invades very seriously the operation of the Civil Service Act, and the government took a very serious responsibility-

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Would the
right hon. gentleman have competitive examinations in the making of these appointments?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
In the case of some of
them, yes. The examination in each case would be made to fit the character of the appointment. It would not necessarily fellow that the examination would be similar to that provided in the case say of a stenographer, the nature of which would be entirely different from an examination that would be applied say to a garage man. For myself, I know of no good reason why scores of these classes included in the order in council of the 29th of June, 1922, were on the government's responsibility exempted from the act.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: What becomes of the competition if you do not have the competitive examination?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: There is an examination, and competitive, too. I say the character of the examination is fitted to the character of the appointment.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman think that the commission is going to advertise every time this class of assistance is needed?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Whenever it is necessary, and they do, so far as I know. I receive every day or so advertisements of the commission for appointments similar to these. The commission are men of brains, they are men of honour; the commission, after all are men who from the mouth of the highest dignitary of this House received two years ago when he was in political opposition to the government that appointed the commission as high an encomium as any public servant could ever deserve. They are men who have never been assailed as having acted in a partisan way, never at any time whatever. They are men who are above partisan criticism at the hands of any man in this country.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: I have not said a word against the commission. I am a supporter of the commission, but I want the law investigated to see if there is anything wrong.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: With a commission of that character, is it not likely they will be able to judge of the qualifications of men for appointments such as this as well as, and, being at the work all this time, better than officers or members of a government? It would appear to me that such would be the case. I know that two members of the commission recommended that the long series of classes be excised from the act. I know not the reason why: I have made no inquiry whatever. But the chairman of that commission, whose presence on the commission is a fact of vital consequence to this country, I know, did not sign the recommendation, and for myself I am disposed to give him credit for not doing so. I do not say that confidence in the commission has been impaired because of this recommendation, but I say here and now that if this class of recommendation goes much further there will not only be apprehension throughout this country, but there will be an impairment of confidence. Responsibility of course is on the government, and I am quite ready to concede that confidence in them will be impaired as well, that is, if the narrow margin that is left can further be reduced. But the commission itself is an institution of permanent consequence to this Dominion, and I earnestly hope, and I express the hope now, that there will not be further recommendations going still more seriously into the scope and operation of the Civil Service Act.	,

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Were there some exemptions made on August 14, 1919?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: There may have been; I do not remember. There were some narrow exceptions made.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: All under $200 were exempted.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: I do not know why they are exempted again if they were exempted then, because all under $200 are exempted by this order of June, 1922. It may be that this is a comprehensive order including all that went before, but I do not think it is so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: I think it is.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
If so, it would have been better if the fact had been referred to in the order itself. There were some exemptions up to December, 1921, but the whole effect of them was very small indeed compared with the enormous scope of this order of the 29th of June, 1922. In this connection let me say that if the commission feels still that there should be other exceptions not included here to which no objection could be
The Civil Service

taken if they were exempted from the operation of the act-I do not know of any myself, but if the commission feels that there are, they have power now to make recommendation, and the government on its responsibility has power to approve of such exceptions. But what the government want if they intend to narrow the scope of the operation of the act, is to walk into the commissioner's office and against the will and advice of the commission, and against the experience of these years, take whole classes of appointments out of the operation of the act. This must be in the mind of the administration if they intend to contract further the scope of operations, because so far as the commission is concerned, it has ample power at the present time to make recommendations to this end.
Now I want to say it is not a matter to be wondered at, after the government of this country exempts these large numbers from the operation of the act, that men in this country in high positions who are indeed deeply interested in the perpetuation of the merit system as a real merit system, and not a farce, should take alarm. No man should be criticised because he takes alarm or because he attributes some of his fears to the action of the government in approving that recommendation. A man should not even be criticised for doing so, but the Prime Minister comes to this House and charges "false representations" against a respectable and highly gifted citizen of this country, the head of Upper Canada College. Because, forsooth, the head of Upper Canada College declared that political forces were at work to bring back the reign of patronage in this country, and because he pointed to the fact that already ten thousand had been brought back from the operation of the act, the Prime Minister declared that he was guilty of a "false representation," and intimated such 10 p.m. an assertion was inconsistent with Dr. Grant's claim to be engaged in a moral reform. In the first place, Dr. Grant has said nothing about "moral reform." This was merely attributed to him to suit the purpose of the Prime Minister. Now the Prime Minister cannot point to a line, he cannot point to a sentence in Dr. Grant's utterance that is not true, that is not undeniably true, that no person who takes himself seriously could dispute for a moment. Does anyone deny that the forces of political patronage are at work? Has anyone listened to this debate and come to any other conclusion? Is there any other inference frtnn the speech of the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), 
or from the speech of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power)?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Is there anything insidious in my speech?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: I did not say insidious

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: The complaint was of insidious influences.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: The hon. member has lost the point altogether. Does anyone, I say, who has listened to the speech of the hon. member dispute that the forces of political patronage are at work to restore the reign of patronage? That is what Dr. Grant said, and because he said it, he is declared to have been guilty of false representation by the Prime Minister of this country. I think the Prime Minister owes to this House, and owes to Dr. Grant, the duty of standing frankly before parliament before whom he made that declaration and apologizing to Dr. Grant.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
What is more, that is the judgment of men of independent thought of this country. Are men outside of parliament to be lampooned in parliament for stating what is manifestly true? There is no inference here that anybody could find fault with or dispute; neither is there any inference beyond the clear meaning of the words themselves. Because 10,000 are gone, that itself, he says, is an argument to show the political forces of patronage are at work. Such is the inference and the only inference that can be drawn from his remarks. The Prime Minister says, "The inference is that we went to the Civil Service Commission and forced them to make the recommendation." Dr. Grant's words admit of no such inference in the world. Whether the fact is true or not, no such inference can be drawn from his remarks. Dr. Grant evidently knew that the government when it passed the order in council aproving the recommendation took upon itself the responsibility of removing 10,000, and the fact, he says, that the government took the responsibility of removing 10,000 goes to prove that the forces of political patronage were at work. And if he wanted confirmation, all he would require to do would be to read the Hansard of two days ago or come and listen to this debate to-night.
Now what this House decides is whether the principle of that act is to remain. Some hon. gentlemen who have spoken have used words consistent only with the determination that the Civil Service Commission shall go altogether. I do not say that all the lan-

The Civil Service
guage of the Prime Minister is consistent only with that view. Some of it is consistent only with such a view, but other language of the Prime Minister is consistent with the opinion that what he wants is the commission to remain but to exist as a mere approving body, a body whose duty it is to examine the qualifications of men and then to leave the government free to make its selection. Some of his language is consistent with such an idea: other of his language is consistent only with an opinion on his part that the real functions of the Civil Service Commission should go altogether.
Now the Prime Minister said at other times "I do not want the commission to go. I do not want patronage to return. I want the commission to remain." But there is not a line in his speech consistent with having the commission remain clothed with any powers which are effective for the purpose of appointments. For this reason I am opposed to any committee. I am opposed to a committee that is launched from this House with the manifesto of the Prime Minister, as spoken the other night. So far as my influence in parliament is effective, I am determined that if this government is powerless to build, it ift least will not be permitted to destroy.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) has purported to quote from my remarks in a previous stage of the debate, words which he sought to construe as equivalent to an expression on my part that the Civil Service Act should be repealed, and also that the Civil Service Commission should be abolished. How fairly and how widely he quoted, I will permit the House to judge by reading the sentences immediately preceding the sentences which he quoted.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: I read his words when he said the Civil Service Commission should remain, and apply the merit system, and I commented on what he had in mind on that occasion.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
He read part of my words, but not all. He took good care to omit, at the outset of his remarks, the sentence which I shall read, which precedes the paragraph he quoted. He quoted first from page 362 of Hansard. Immediately after referring to the motion introduced by the hon. member for Quebec (Mr. Power) I said:
I think it would be a great mistake to repeal the Civil Service Act.
Those are my words. My right hon. friend never quoted them to the House. I again give them to the House as expressing my view with respect to the Civil Service Act. I think it would be a great mistake to have the Civil Service Act repealed. That refers to the act which is on the statutes at the present time.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: I did not say the hon. minister wanted it repealed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
I think hon. members will agree that my right hon. friend sought to have it appear that I would like to have the Civil Service Commission-abolished. He did not read the following words, which appear on page 365 of Hansard-
I hope I have made it very clear that I would strongly oppose any move to abolish the Civil Service Commission.
The second statement which I have just read was made when I spoke after recess. The previous statement had been made before recess. Both times I made my position very clear, that I was entirely opposed to the repeal of the Civil Service Act and entirely opposed to the abolition of the Civil Service Commission. But I did make the statement that I thought it was desirable to have the present Civil Service Act amended, and I gave as my reason for it that the government during the period between sessions, in its desire to effect economies and further efficiency in the public service, had had conferences with both the Civil Service Commission and the deputy ministers, and that, as a result of those conferences, as well as of experience gained in the work of administration, the government was persuaded that the Civil Service Act could be amended to the advantage of the public service. It was in that connection that I advocated a reference of the act to a committee of this parliament.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in order that there may be no misunderstanding as to where I stand in this matter, and as to where the government stands, despite all the efforts of hon. members opposite to have it appear to the contrary, may I state emphatically, that we are opposed to the repeal of the Civil Service	Act,	that	we	are opposed	tothe abolition of the Civil Service Commission,	but	that	we	believe it to	be
in the public interest that the Civil Service Act should be looked into by a committee of this House, with power to make recommendations to parliament; and that amendments to the act which may commend themselves to the judgment of this House should be passed. That is the position of the government. I do not think I can make it any plainer.
The Civil Service

Then, my hon. friend said that I had made charges against Dr. Grant, the principal of Upper Canada College, and that I ought publicly to apologize to Dr. Grant in this parliament. May I read to my hon. friend just what I said about Dr. Grant? I think I confined my reference pretty largely to his own words. I drew the attention of the House to the fact that a good deal of the feeling with respect to the Civil Service Commission, and the government's relation thereto was the result of a statement attributed to the Chairman of the Civil Service Commission in an address delivered in the city of Toronto, which was copied by the press of this country from one end to the other. This statement was to the effect that some 10,000 had been withdrawn from under the operation of the Civil Service Commission, and that this was due to the insidious action of politicians, implying the government in power. Let me read the words Dr. Roche was supposed to have uttered which appear in direct quotations in the press reports to which I am referring. I ask hon. members in their own minds to determine what the meaning and purport of these words are. Dr. Roche is reported in the paper in direct quotation as speaking as follows:
The fate of this law however-
That is the Civil Service law-
-"however, is beset with dangers due to the insidious, unseen and silent manipulations of the adherents of patronage in political life," he said. "Slowly, but surely, the politicians will gain back to their own control more and more of the service by the process of exemptions. On June 29 last an order in council was passed exempting from the operation of the merit law a great many positions, which affects in all 10,000 persons out of a total of 50,000 employees, thus placing back into patronage one-fifth of the whole public service.
The effort at present is aimed at the return to patronage of the system of promotions which at present has been so splendidly developed by the Civil Service Commission. Technical positions are also under immediate attack, and there can be no doubt that the whole merit law is in danger unless the strong arm of public opinion is organized to oppose its attack.
These are the words which were publicly read as having been uttered by Dr. Roche, Chairman of the Civil Service Commission. I ask hon. gentlemen of this House, are these words capable of any interpretation in the minds of a reading public, other than that Dr. Roche was protesting against the action of the government in withdrawing 10,000 appointees from under its jurisdiction? Those statements are false. These are not true statements.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: What statements?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
What I have
just read.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Which ones?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
The whole
business is false. In the first place there is no one prepared to say how many persons were withdrawn from under the operation of the provisions of the Civil Service Act in virtue of the order which my hon. friend has read, and which was in reality the recommendation of the commission.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Does he say that the
number 10,000 is wrong?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
I say I believe it is wrong. I think the figures are a mere guess. I could not say whether 5,000 or 2,000 is nearer the mark. I say they were used without any knowledge on the part of the person who used them; the numbers were called in question and also the inference. But I am prepared to leave it to the judgment of fairminded members of this House as to whether, reading that statement, at the time it appeared, the reader would not believe that Dr. Roche was protesting against the withdrawing of a number of positions, whatever the number may have been, from the control of the Civil Service Commission and making it appear that they were being withdrawn at the instance of the government, when, as a matter of fact, they were withdrawn at the instance of the Civil Service Commission itself. If my hon. friend will let me have the order to which he has referred, I will quote from it the reason for the commission's action as it appears in the commission's recommendation:
The Civil Service Commission is of opinion that it is not practicable to prescribe a system of competitive examinations or tests as required by the Civil Service Act.
The Civil Service Commission made that statement in the recommendation they sent to council asking that the positions enumerated should be exempted from their control. They stated they did not believe it was practicable to prescribe competitive examinations or tests. My right hon. friend asks about the government assuming responsibility. Certainly we assume responsibility. But, what would our responsibility have been if, after the Civil Service Commission's recommendation of the withdrawal of these classes because it was not practicable to hold examinations, the government had refused to accept the recommendation of the commission and compelled that body to go on with the system of advertising positions and holding examinations? We would have been found guilty, and rightfully guilty of being negligent in the matter of caring for economies in the public service.

Now what does Dr. Grant say? Here is Dr. Grant's letter to Dr. Roche. I will quote just one paragraph. The letter is dated "Upper Canada College, Toronto, December 21, 1922," and the paragraph in question reads:
The items complained of-
And the passage that I have read contained the items complained of-	[DOT]
-were not in your speech at all,-
This is what Dr. Grant writes to Dr. Roche-
-but in a memorandum circulated by me on my own responsibility,-

speechtext: He is a liar then.

speechtext: Order.

speechtext:
(reading):
-and sent to the press on the day before your address, in the hope of stirring up interest in it, and in the possible formation of a National Civil Service Reform League, which I have much at heart. The Globe reporter, who had your speech as an "assignment", evidently acted in a way familiar to all journalists, and wrote his report from my memorandum: the report consequently bears no relation to your speech as actually delivered.
Then Dr. Grant goes on to say:
Your speech contained no reference whatever to the 10,000 civil servants exempted from the operation of the Act. It was a model of good taste and reticence. No human being could have told from it that you had ever belonged to a political party or whether your relations with the present government as chairman of the Civil Service Commission were better or worse than they had been with previous governments. Personally, I had a natural longing for a little more "spice".
There is the statement that Dr. Grant has written to Dr. Roche and my right hon. friend says that I ought to apologize to Dr. Grant!

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: It would be a shame to do it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Well, I only hope my right hon. friend will always be as ready to apologize.
Mr. Speaker, while these various classes have been withdrawn from under the control of the Civil Service Act and the Civil Seivice Commission, they have been withdrawn, as I have already intimated, because of the commission's mention of the following:
The Civil Service Commission is of opinion that it is not practicable to prescribe a system of competitive examinations or tests as required by the Civil Service Act.
However, even with respect to these appointments, the commission goes on to lay down certain requirements by which the government is bound and which forms a part of
the same order. My right hon. friend did not refer to this. Let me read what it says:
The commission is further of opinion that there is good ground for believing that the above classes were among those which parliament had in mind for exemption in amending the Civil Service Act during the Session of 1921-
In pther words the Civil Service Commission assumes there its responsibility to parliament and says that when it recomlnends the withdrawal of these particular classes, it believes it is doing what parliament had in mind. To continue:
-and the Civil Service. Commission therefore, has the honour to report that it is not practicable to apply the Civil Service Act to the classes mentioned above and to recommand that they be excluded from the operation of the Act and dealt with in accordance with the following procedure:
1.	That the selection of employees for the above classes shall be left entirely in the hands of the departments, subject to the following conditions:
(a)	That the appointment is necessary for the efficient carrying on of the work of the department.
(b)	That the preference extended by section 39 of the Civil Service Act 1918, as amended, shall be observed.
(c)	That the person selected shall satisfy the department as to his qualifications.
(d)	That he shall be suitable as to age, character and habits.
2.	That the compensation shall not exceed the salaries provided in the classification schedules, and that where "Prevailing Rates" are provided as the compensation for a class, or where no class schedule exists, the rates of pay shall be such as are recommended by the department and approved by the Governor General in Council, and that the compensation in these cases shall carry no bonus.
Provided that, where any position which is exempted under the provisions of section 38B of the Civil Service Act. 1918, as amended, (with the exception of those in groups 1 and 2) is to be continued for more than six months, the department shall report the duties thereof to the commission in order that the position may be classified and that no further payment of salary in connection with the same shall be authorized until the position shall be so classified.
Provided further that a report shall be made by every department to the Civil Service Commission in the months of January, April, July and October in each year, setting out the name, duties, salary, place of residence and place of employment of each person appointed under the authority of these regulations during the preceding three months, with the date of commencing duty and the probable duration of employment. In each case where the employee has been on military service overseas, the letters "O.A.S." should be added after the name.
Is it not evident that the report which I have just read to the House far from being capable of bearing the inference that the government had sought in any way to return to patronage by carrying out the recommendation of the commission is capable only of bearing the inference that the government in the action that it has taken has sought to carry out the recommendation of the commission in giving expression to the wishes of parliament as the commission itself interpreted them. effort to have it appear that the government is desirous of returning to patronage is well understood. We all understand the purpose of it, we all know the reason of it. I am sure that no hon. member of the House, who has any responsibility, would welcome a return to patronage where it can be avoided. I would like, however, to say this: There are even fewer members of the House who, having positions of responsibility, would like to be held responsible for appointments in the making of which, in many cases, they had absolutely no voice. That is a different situation. There are two sides to the case and I am putting both sides to the House in order that hon. members may understand them.
My right hon. friend has drawn attention to the fact that this recommendation was signed by two members of the commission. Most of the recommendations that come from the commission are signed in that way. I ask my right hon. friend does he repudiate the signatures that are on this recommendation? The signatures are those of the appointees of his own government, they are not the appointees of this government. We have accepted the members of the commission just as we found them. We have made no change whatever in the personnel of the commission. A recommendation comes to us from them and we put it through. This recommendation is from the right hon. gentleman's own appointees. What I have said should be a sufficient answer to the representations made by hon. gentlemen opposite to the effect that we wish to return to patronage.
Now my right hon. friend asks what is the object of the government in asking that the Civil Service Act should be referred to a committee. He asks "Is anyone so innocent as to believe that the motive is that which the government has expressed it to be?"

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: The signatures to the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission, I understand, are those of Mr. LaRochelle and Mr. Jameson. I was under the impression and I am sure it will be confirmed, that we did not appoint Mr. LaRochelle but that he was appointed by the Laurier government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Perhaps I
should have intimated that Mr. LaRochelle was appointed years ago, was continued in office by my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen), and was a member of the commission during the time he was in power. To that extent I am prepared to stand corrected.
But now, as to the motive the government had, I thought I had made that clear when

I spoke before. I said that during the recess between sessions the government had given serious attention to the important question of efficiency and economy in the public service. I said that the government had invited, into conference with its members, both the commission and the deputy ministers, and that both the commission and the deputy ministers had expressed the view that the Civil Service Act was capable of amendment in particulars that would make it a better working and more efficient instrument for the purposes for which it was intended. In addition to that, the government imposed on the deputy ministers a special obligation to report to it with respect to the workings of the Civil Serivce Act, and more particularly with respect to economies and efficiency in the different departments of government. Prior to the framing of the Estimates the government sought to have each of the deputy ministers go carefully with the officers of the various branches, into the whole question of the numbers of their staffs with a view of seeing where it would be possible to cut down. Hon. gentlemen ask us to reduce the numbers of the civil service. What would they say if ministers began to make changes in the civil service without consulting with the deputy ministers? The deputy ministers are the permanent heads; they are part of the service itself; and the government is bound to act with respect to the numbers of the service more or less on their advice. Every minister is more or less obliged to take the word of his deputy as to the requirements of his particular staff, and the extent of its personnel. After the conference with the government, the deputy ministers grouped themselves into a body for the purpose of making a joint report to the government. I have in my hand the report which was submitted by a committee of the deputy ministers, and which bears the names of the following gentlemen:
Messrs. W. W. Cory, E. L. Newcombe, R. M. Coulter. Major G. A. Bell, Lt.-Col. N. F. Parkinson, J. H. Grisdale, J. B. Hunter, F. C. T. O'Hara, A. Johnston and F. A. Acland.
I will ask the House to bear with me a few moments while I read extracts from this report, as therein will appear the reason why the government has suggested the advisability of a committee of parliament hearing the deputy ministers before any recommendations are made as to changes in the Civil Service Act. The report reads in part:
The Committee of Deputy Ministers, appointed at a meeting held on the 30tli June, 1922, at the instance of the government to consider matters affecting the Civil Service of Canada, begs respectfully to report that the various departments have been consulted in this connection, that the material gathered has been carefully

The Civil Service
analyzed and that the following is a precis of the recommendations which have been adopted. The scope of the activities of the committee embraced the following subjects, namely:-
(a)	Appointments;
(b)	Promotions;
(c)	Classification of positions;
(d)	Transfers;
(e)	Leave of absence;
(f)	Cost of living bonus;
(g)	Whitley Councils;
(h)	Superannuation;
(i)	Reduction of staff.
Then there are quoted three subsections of section 43 of the Civil Service Act. The report continues:
The effect of this section is to place all appointments of whatever nature they may be, under the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission and your Committee is of the opinion that its provisions should be amended in the following direction:-
"That appointments to professional and technical positions, or to those of assistant deputy ministers, heads of branches and all officials in the higher gradeg, say those appointed to positions for which the minimum compensation is $2,400.00 per annum or over, be made by the Governor General in Council on the recommendation of the head of the department based on a report in writing from the deputy head."
Your committee also desires to offer the following recommendation, namely:-
"That there are certain outside services, such as employees in offices outside of Canada, rural postmasters, etc., as to which it is impracticable to apply the provisions of the Civil Service Act reasonably, and these should be removed from the application of the Act, a list of such services to be supplied by the various departments."
Section (b) deals with promotions. It quotes the sections in the Civil Service Act with regard to promotions and then goes on:
Your committee considers that the best interests of the service require that promotion should be departmentally regulated, and recomn^end therefore,
"That the present Civil Service provisions with regard to promotions be repealed and that there be substituted therefor a provision to the effect that promotions shall be made for merit by the Governor General in Council upon the recommendation of the head of the department, based on a report in writing from the deputy head, and accompanied by a certificate of qualification, by the Civil Service Commission.
Section (c) deals with the 'classification of positions: The report reads:
The Civil Service Commission has provided a complicated classification which, besides being a positive hindrance to effective administration, requires special study properly to understand. This is more especially illustrated in the case of clerical assistance which is subdivided into scores of special classes, the qualifications for many of which are practically the same, i.e., the incumbent of any of these might readily perform the duties of the other clerical positions.
Your committee considers,-
"That this complicated classification should be repealed and that the Civil Service be divided into a number of classes on lines similar to those established by the Civil Service Act of 1908 or 1918."
36i
Then there is a part of the report dealing with transfers and yet another with leave of absence. The latter is worded as follows:
The Civil Service Commission should make workable . regulations with regard to leave of absence, but the administration of the same should be left entirely in the hands of the deputy ministers who are in a better position than the commission to pass judgment on the applications submitted to them.
There are also sections dealing with the cost of living bonus, Whitley councils, and superannuation. On the subject of the reduction of staff, the report reads:
The committee has given careful thought to the question of reduced expenditure. This is a matter which lies in a measure within the authority of the deputy ministers with relation of existing governmental services; new legislation, however, frequently entails new services and the most rigid economy may not prevent increased expenditures. It has been sometimes suggested that the government service is at the present time functioning on an abnormal basis, the outcome of an unnatural development of the Great War, and that every effort should be made to return to a normal or pre-war basis. The committee has learned that reports on these matters have been in the case of many departments forwarded by the departmental heads directly to the Prime Minister; also that the views expressed by the Prime Minister in his remarks to the deputy ministers with regard to the desirability of bringing about a substantial reduction in the public expenditure have received careful attention and that much has been already accomplished along the lines indicated. It must not be, however, overlooked that many years have passed since 1914, the date usually accepted as indicating normal conditions, and during these years the growth of the business connected with the permanent and essential services of government has been considerable; and moreover new departments or branches of the service, growing directly out of the war itself, have been established, as, for instance, in the case of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, Soldier Settlement Board, Pensions Boards, etc., and also many new statutes have been enacted which have to be administered, requiring addition to the staff. Precise comparisons with previous periods therefore become difficult. The committee, however, realises the intent of the Prime Minister's remarks with regard to these matters, and is able to state with some confidence that the departments generally are doing what is possible to secure the largest possible degree of economy in the public administration.
The report eoneludes:
It is obvious that the adoption of the recommendations of the report would eliminate expensive services which are wholly concerned in the making and enforcement of artificial requirements regulating appointments, promotions, transfers and the equipment generally of the staff requisite for the discharge of the essential duties of government, and in the view of the committee this very considerable saving may be effected without in any wise impairing the standard and efficiency of the service, while at the same time avoiding the delays and inconveniences incident to the references to the Civil Service Commission, which the present regulations require.
The committee was appointed on the 30tli of June, 1922. and submitted its report on the 4th day of December, 1922.

Will the minister state
whether or not the signatures of the deputy-ministers whose names appear on the report are affixed to the report and whether or not they take responsibility for all the deputy ministers?

It is signed by the chairman of the committee. All the deputy minsiters whose names I have mentioned take responsibility for the report.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Do the others?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: As far as I am aware this committee embraces all the deputy ministers who were in the city at the time. All were invited to the conference and all were asked to join in the report. There must be a few names omitted. Why, I do not know. Possibly they were not in the city. There may be other reasons for the absence of their names from the committee. They may have authorized others mentioned to act on their behalf.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Maybe I misunderstand
my right hon. friend. Is the committee a committee of all the deputy ministers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
The government asked all the deputy ministers to meet it in conference. The deputy ministers came and conferred with the government in the council chamber. We went very fully into the whole question of the conditions in the service and the possible reduction of the staffs. We asked for a frank expression of views on the part of the deputies as to the working of the civil service regulations. We got very full and free expressions of opinions from the deputy ministers. We then asked them as a body to prepare a report for the government; to constitute themselves a committee for the purpose; to make such recommendations to the government, as in their opinion seemed to be advisable to improve the efficiency of and to effect economies in the public service. This is the document we have received, it purports to be, and I believe is, a report of all the deputy ministers.
Having this report in its hand the government might have proceeded, as some hon. gentlemen have suggested, we might have proposed amendments to the Civil Service Act in accordance with these recommendations. I ask hon. members who have listened to this debate, what would have been the first criticism levelled at the government if it had taken that step? We would have been told,

and the country would have been led to believe, that we were seeking a return to patronage. The country would never believe we were trying to effect economies and to promote efficiency in the public service. This is not a report from the government but a report to the government from the heads of the Civil Service itself, .and it is the class of recommendations contained in this report that, we submit, might reasonably be considered as possible amendments to the Civil Service Act at the present time. Who is to know of the effective working of the act . better than those who are responsible for administering the different departments?
Let me now come to the last point, because I feel I have spoken at too great length already. Why did I suggest to my hon. friend the other day that this matter should be referred to a committee of parliament? Well,
I might answer-although the reason was not in my mind at the time, but it is -suggested by what my right hon. friend has said about the Civil Service Commission-that parliament or a committee of parliament is a body to which the commission should report. He says that the commission is not responsible to the government, but to parliament. Well, all that this amendment asks is that the commission which is responsible to parliament be given an opportunity to appear before a committee of this House and report to its members upon this very matter. Are hon. gentlemen going to vote against that? Is my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen), after he says that . this commission is responsible to parliament, going to refuse a committee of this House the right to hear representations from the deputy ministers and members of the Civil Service Commission with respect to the very act for the working of which they are responsible? That is one of the reasons we ask for a committee-that the Civil Service Commission should be given a chance to appear before a committee of parliament to which my hon. friend says it is responsible.
But there is another reason, and it is the one which governed me in the matter. At the very opening of the session one or two hon. gentlemen opposite referred to the attitude which the government had adopted toward the House. They expressed appreciation of the circumstance that before proposing legislation on many matters that were of concern to the country as a whole we had invited the opinion of parliament, that we had sought to obtain the views of the different groups, that we were in the open and had sought to afford a full knowledge of the circumstances governing recommendations which we were proposing to embody in our legislation.

The Civil Service
They expressed the hope that the government would not depart from that practice.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Will not the Prime Minister admit that in its initial stages this motion was not introduced by the government but by a private member in a way that was exceedingly antagonistic to hon. members on this side of the House?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
I am very sorry that my hon. friend feels there was any antagonism in the matter. I do not know that he should feel any more aggrieved than the government [DOT] itself. We were not able to accept the recommendation in the form in which it was introduced. It was not a pleasant duty for me to say to my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power) that I could not accept his resolution. But I said so openly, and I do not think hon. gentlemen opposite should feel any more aggrieved in that regard. It was I who made the suggestion that the matter should be referred to a committee of the House, and I am giving hon. gentlemen opposite the reason for the suggestion. Let me say with all candor and frankness that either it is in the .interests of the public to proceed in the way that has been suggested, or it is not. HAn. gentlemen opposite feel that they should be taken as much as possible into the confidence of the government. I am anxious to meet them in that regard. I am anxious to have the reasons for the legislation that goes through this House as thoroughly appreciated by every group as is possible consonant with the government assuming its full responsibility for what it introduces. And I say in regard to such a measure as civil service reform, that this is the very class of measure with respect to which the government would not be justified in assuming a high or arbitrary attitude, but is of the kind which should in the first instance be submitted to a committee of the House composed of members of the different groups.	[DOT]
It is because I am anxious that hon. members who will be criticizing the estimates, who will be finding fault with the fact that there are not more reductions in the Civil [DOT] Service-as my hon. friend from West Cal gary (Mr. Shaw) implied there should be this afternoon-should know why those reductions are not greater than as they appear in the estimates. They will find out the reasons if they will bring the commission and the deputy ministers before them. The government is pretty much in the hands of these two bodies, and all we ask in the matter of effecting economies is that hon. gentlemen
opposite shall know and appreciate to the full what our -difficulties are. If they think that it is perhaps on the whole better for the country to pay out a little more money for examinations, for transfers and for promotions, effected as they are by the Civil Service Commission, that it is going to serve some public interest to spend more money and to keep our staffs a little larger than they need be because of the mass of regulations to be complied with, well and good. We will then be in the position at least of knowing that parliament is with us in our inability to make any further change.
1 wish to say emphatically to hon. members that the government is doing the best it possibly can to effect economies in every direction. This is the direction in which we have found the most difficulty, and I submit that it is in the interests of the country that there should be certain amendments to the Civil Service Act-not amendments arbitrarily suggested by the government, but amendments that may recommend themselves to the intelligence of the groups of this House represented on a special committee. For that reason I am supporting the amendment which has been moved, that the Civil Service Act be made the subject of reference to a committee with power to make such recommendations to this House as it may see fit.
And may I say this in conclusion? After those recommendations have been made, before any change can be effected in the existing law, the recommendations themselves will have to be embodied in the form of draft legislation and considered here on the floor of parliament. What is the cause for alarm in that method of procedure? I submit that if the purpose is a sincere one, that if hon. gentlemen are really in earnest in their desire to have full justice done the deputy ministers in their effort to carry on the work of their departments efficiently and effectively, if they are sincere in their contention that we must seek to carry out economies in the public service, then it is their duty to support the amendment which is now before the House.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had not intended taking any further part in this debate, but the Prime Minister has made some remarks that I think perhaps are levelled just a little at myself.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: No, no.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
I am not taking any offence. The remarks were perfectly fair and perfectly honest. I know I made recommendations along the line on which he spoke. The
The Civil Service

Prime Minister made a very plausible speech in favour of the amendment. I agree with my deskmate, the member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey), that the tone of this debate at its commencement was very different from the tone of it now, and that had some of the speeches made by hon. members on the other side been in line with the Prime Minister's remarks, we might have been prepared to listen with at least a great deal more sympathy and consideration. But in view of the speeches that have been made by hon. gentlemen on the other side, Mr. Speaker, I have been forced to the conclusion that the idea is to lead to nothing less than the repeal of the Civil Service Act. I may be wrong; quite a number of hon. members on the other side have not spoken. I am dealing only with those who have spoken, the tenor of whose remarks was all along the line of getting the patronage back into the hands of members representing the different constituencies.
I saw to-night quite a large volume of evidence that was taken before a commission two years ago-so large a volume that it was useless for me to attempt to master what it contained. I wonder what has happened during the last two years to make it necessary to hear that evidence all over again? Were the deputy ministers not consulted at that time? Did they not give evidence? Were these difficulties not experienced at that time? I do not know. Of course, I have learned something to-night, I admit, from the statement made by the Prime Minister. However, I cannot but believe that the argument advanced by the right hon. leader of the Opposition is sound in the main. I know very well -I do not want to make any insinuations- that it makes quite a difference from which side of the House you speak. Perhaps there was not much temptation for hon. members to my right, when they were in power, to make very many changes in the Civil Service Act; I do not know. At any rate, the temptation may not have been so great then as it is in the case of the present government.
We realize now what recommendations have been made by the deputy ministers, and perhaps they are reasonable. But in view of the feeling that prevails on the other side, and judging from the speeches to which I have listened, I am a little afraid of any report that might be made to this House by a government majority committee in connection with civil service reform. H we could have a committee representing equally the different parties in this House, I would not be so much afraid. I feel that members are perfectly honest in the views which they express; they

are contending for what they think is right. I believe the majority of the members who have spoken really think that the Civil Service would be improved by their having some power to make appointments. However, while 1 should approve of the idea of a committee to consider many other subjects, I cannot see my way clear to withdraw from the stand I have already taken in this respect. I know very well that a good many hon. members on this side will not vote with me; it is entirely a matter for themselves to judge. I am speaking only on my own behalf, and not on behalf of the party that I have the honour to lead.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not the privilege to be in the House during the first two days of this debate. However, I considered the matter of sufficient importance to justify my reading the whole of the discussion as it appeared in Hansard, and I came to certain conclusions. After listening to the debate to-day I see no reason to come to a different conclusion from that which I reached after reading the report of the first two days' debate.
I have noticed more than once since coming to this House evidences of the fact that the government might well pray to be saved from its friends. We noticed that last year when, on the question of the government ownership and operation of railways, certain supporters of the government took occasion to launch out at great length against the principle of government ownership. I felt that if I were a member of the Liberal caucus I would want to discipline the members who made such an exhibition on that occasion. It is not calculated to create confidence on the part of the people in the giving of government ownership a fair chance to have supporters of the government speaking as they did at that time.
I think we have another illustration here to-night: the government might well pray to be saved from its friends. Undoubtedly the member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) expressed what were his own ideas when he moved that resolution. I have no doubt that when it was put upon the order paper it was expressive of his view that the Civil Service Act should be abolished. I think it was somewhat unfortunate that the rules of the House compelled the Speaker to rule that the motion could not be changed as the hon. member suggested. The ruling was no doubt in harmony with precedent, and I make no criticism on that score, except that had it been different the discussion would have been sim-

The Civil Service
plified. However, we know where the member for Quebec South stands.
Then, other members say they do not want to go that far but wish to turn to the act of 1908, which would take the outside service away from the Civil Service Commission. Unfortunately a great deal that has been said in support of the resolution has certainly left upon many hon. members the impression ihat the desire is to go back to patronage as far as it is possible to do so. There is a Scotch expression like this: "We get the meanin' by the mumpin.' " And it seemed to me the "mumpin' " was sufficiently strong in certain quarters to give us an idea of what was in the minds of some hon. members. It cannot be wondered at, therefore, that we in this corner of the House came to the conclusion that hon. members supporting the resolution, including my good friend from King's, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes), for whom I have learned to entertain a very high respect, wished to go back to the old system. I know they managed to clothe the patronage system in some beautiful garments; undoubtedly they gave to Satan the appearance of an angel of light.
We should remember that this patronage question has two faces. So far we have dealt only with the matter of appointments. The other side of the question was the one that aroused the most abhorrence in the minds of fair men, namely, that of dismissals. Many sordid things took place in the matter of dismissals from office, especially of persons in the outside service. It was not an uncommon thing during an election campaign to have members going around with an appointment in their pockets, and if the time came when the persons making promises of jobs were in a position to implement them, why, good and faithful servants were dismissed from office without very much consideration being shown to them. I do not know that one party was more guilty than another. I can go back as far as 1911, and I have one case in mind-it was some years after 1911 because it hung fire for a long time-where a public servant who had two sons in the army was dismissed while his sons were overseas. Now it is things of that kind which have raised the antagonism of the people of this country to the old system of patronage.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Who did that?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
It was done during war
time.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: What year?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Before 1921 anyway. That is only one illustration of the kind of thing
which has made people revolt against any thought of going back to the old patronage system. These dismissals were generally made on the ground of offensive partisanship, and therein in the past we have been guilty of a good [DOT] deal of hypocrisy. I recall one instance under a former administration where, when it was pointed out that certain persons had been guilty of offensive partisanship the reply was made "They are not Offensive to us," and that disposed of the matter. Now if partisanship is an offence, then let us say so. 1 might make complaints of offensive partisanship in the last election. There were some whose partisanship was offensive to me I know, but I have not made any complaints hitherto in the matter.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Is my hon. friend aware that section 32 of the Civil Service Act provides that:
No deputy head, officer, clerk or employee in the Civil Service shall be debarred from voting at any dominion or provincial election if, under the laws governing the said election, he has the right to vote; but no such deputy head, officer, clerk or employee shall engage in partisan work in connection with any such election, or contribute, receive or in any way deal with any money for any party funds.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
That, of course, refers
particularly to the inside service.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: It refers to both the inside and the outside.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Does it refer to postmasters and custom house officers?

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: Certainly.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: All I know is that I have a postmaster in mind who has taken refuge under what he supposed to be the protection of the Civil Service Act, and I say that his partisanship was somewhat offensive to me, although I have never made any complaint. But here is the point I want to make: If this parliament decides that civil servants shall not take part in political affairs beyond exercising their franchise at the polls, let us say so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext: That is the law now.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
In that case let it not be considered an act of partisanship justifying dismissal from office until the offender is known to have transgressed the law, and let it not be left to the government that happens to be in power simply to dismiss from the service those whose partisanship has been offensive to itself and not at all those offen-
The Civil Service

sive to the party on the other side. It is on . this question of dismissals that 11 p.m. the ire of the public has been particularly aroused. I understand human nature well enough to realize something of the resentment that hon. gentlemen oppostie, we will say, feel when they know that dismissals have been made and the positions filled by those who were just as truly partisans as the ones dismissed, and in many cases more so. That is a question w'fe might very well consider.
When the question of appointing a committee was suggested, I might say that the suggestion appealed to me, and after reading the speeches that were delivered during two days debate of the subject, my conclusion was that it was a reasonable request to make of this House. The deputy ministers had made certain recommendations, and the commissioners themselves had made certain recommendations, and I came to the conclusion that the request for a committee of this House was a reasonable one, and that we ought to be willing to meet them. To-day's debate has not in any wise altered my opinion upon that point. At the same time I would point out that if in any large degree that committee should be composed of those who have advocated extreme views in regard to the question of patronage, it might very well mean that those of us who hold other views might have to retire from the committee at once in the event of our being appointed. But it does seem to me that the proposition is a reasonable one that we should express a willingness to meet those who are charged with the administration of the act, and whom we might very well suppose to be competent to give some information as to the way in which that act ought to be amended. Personally I am absolutely opposed to any return to patronage in the old form or in any form. At the same time I can quite believe it possible that the present act is not absolutely perfect and that it is capable of amendment. I think the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) put it very pertinently when he asked the hon. member for Calgary "Was not the British Civil Service Act brought to its present state of perfection by a series of amendments?" or something to that effect. Though the act may have been of good service up to the present time, I am quite prepared to believe that it may be capable of rendering better service, and for my part I could not justify myself in taking a position which would seem to indicate that I have no desire for any further information on the subject.
[MY. Brown.]

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs

My hon. friend suggests an entire change in the procedure of the House. It has always been customary to have the chairman appointed from the government side and for the government to be represented on the committee in proportion to its majority in the House. That has been the procedure for years.
May I also point out that any recommendations the committee may make wall have to be considered by the House. The government has not such a large majority in the House that it will be able to drive anything through; and after the legislation has passed this Chamber it has to go to the Senate, where again the government has not such a majority that it can force any of its measures through.

subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
There has been considerable criticism of the mover of this resolution, some of it, if I were to use the words of the hon. gentleman for Springfield (Mr. Hoey), rather antagonistic, and some of it, perhaps, actuated by the prejudices of the moment. The hon. leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) has stated that he would, per-

The Civil Service
haps, have consented to give a favourable vote on the amendment had it not been for the remarks made by some hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) a man whom I respect, has almost challenged me to say that I was opposed to the Civil Service Commission. I stated very distinctly that I was.
I do not think he should try to make opposition to the Civil Service Commission a crime. It strikes me that he wishes to add to the considerable number of crimes which are already enacted in our statute books; but to accuse me of the crime of lese majeste because I do not think the Civil Service Commission is a body to administer the affairs of this country is, I think, going a little too far.
I have listened to the debate in vain to hear one solid argument urged against the contention which was made by some hon. members on this side of the House, that it was not good business to have an outside commission name employees to positions of trust and to positions in which executive ability is required. It is true one hon. member stated that there was this distinction between business and the affairs of a political department, that business men were born to the job. The commissioners in charge of the Civil Service must be reborn, because at least two of them took a very active part in politics >
before becoming commissioners of the Civil Service. The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) stated that there was this distinction; that after all business was not quite the same as politics, that you could not introduce the same methods in politics that you could in business. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that that is the aim and object of this government, and of the party that supports it,-to introduce business methods in the government of this country, and if the hon leader of the Opposition found it impossible to do that, then let him, at anj rate, give somebody else a chance to do something along that line. I have not heard any real argument to destroy the contention that the present system in many cases is not practicable.
We have heard a great deal from hon. members about the evils of the spoils system, about the electorate of this country being debauched. but we have not heard any hon. member tell us honestly that he thought the Civil Service Commission sitting in Ottawa could efficiently and judiciously make the appointments of labourers in British Columbia or in the far eastern provinces of Canada. We have not heard it urged that we, the members of this parliament, were right in putting out of our own jurisdiction the affairs of the civil servants of. Canada. I pleaded for what I
thought was responsible government, for government that would be responsible to the people, and in reply I heard from the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) that this same argument was used fifty years ago.
I never claimed that the argument or the idea, was original. Does the hon. gentleman from Calgary not know that fifty or a "hundred years ago people died for the cause of responsible government? If the hon. member has read history-and I know he has, because he is an astute lawyer and he has literary taste- he will know that for many years the politicians of Great Britain and of Canada were agitated by that very question of responsible government, and I am not at all displeased when he tells me that I have returned to the arguments which were used by our forefathers, and for which they are constantly being praised and lauded, even in this House.
Reference was made to the remarks which I made in 1921, when this Civil Service Amendment Act came up for discussion in this House. I do not suppose the hon. member for Calgary West who so charitably referred to my stand at that time, had taken the trouble to read these remarks. For his benefit, if not for the benefit of the other members of the House. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that you will permit m* to read portions of my remarks on that occasion. I said:
On behalf of certain of my constituents who voted for hon. gentlemen opposite, believing in their promises to carry on the public services in a way in which they had not hitherto been carried on and that thereby the abuses of patronage would be abolished, I think I have a perfect right to register my protest. It is our duty to see that hon. gentlemen opposite are not guilty of any backsliding, that once having entered on the path of reform and of uplift they shall continue to the end of their days, which we all believe will be soon.
I protested on behalf of certain of my constituents who supported the leader of the Opposition. These supporters of the Opposition leader apparently did not think that my work on their behalf was sufficient, because I am sure the great majority of them actually voted against me at the last election. Therefore, I think my hon. friend from Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) will be quite willing to admit that I am freed of any obligation which I might have had towards them at any rate.
To be more serious for a moment after having listened very attentively to the speech of the leader of the Opposition I have come to the conclusion that his reason for opposing a reference of this matter to a committee is very similar to that which I gave some days ago for opposing the amendments to the act which he introduced in 1921. I said then that I did not trust the Tories. After having carefully considered the speech of the leader of the Opposition I have come to the conclu-
The Civil Service

sion that his reason for not supporting the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) is that he does not trust the Grits. He states at great length that it may be very well for us to have a committee, but that behind this demand for the appointment of a committee there is the insidious influence-he did not use those words, but that is what he meant-of those of us here who do not approve of, who do not believe in, the Civil Service Commission. He says "On our side of the House we knew when we brought* down this legislation what we wanted. We merely wanted to amend the act, and nobody on our side of the House attacked the Civil Service Commission." I wonder if he heard, or if he read, the speech of the hon. member of West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) during the debate? His speech was so bitter an attack on the Civil Service Commission that he was constantly called to order. I wonder if he read the speech of the Hon. Mr. Edwards or the speech of Mr. Currie, or the speech of Mr. Fripp during that debate? Surely if he is entitled to doubt our bona fides to-day we are entitled to doubt his motives at that time.

What I said was that no member of the government, in any speech, intimated the least thought of abolishing the active work of the commission, or of restricting it in any respect whatever.
