subsubtopic: MOTION BY MR. POWER FOR REPEAL OF THE CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
If it is quite fair for the leader of the Opposition to make references to the speeches of the members of the government at that time it is quite fair for me to refer to the speeches of those who then sup-
ported the government, and to draw the same inference after reading the speeches of hon. members who supported my right hon. friend.
At the time this resolution was introduced, I, at least, allowed it to be understood that I did not expect to obtain the support of the majority of the members of the House. I stated frankly what my views on the subject were, and some other hon. members have done the same thing. I frankly believe that we cannot get the most efficient service out of the Civil Service Act as at present framed. There may be only a few of us on this side that believe it. There may be more than that number, but I am under the impression there will only be a few. That is no reason for hon. members opposite refusing to the government the opportunity which it asks of obtaining before a committee a full and free discussion of the different situations which have been created by the Civil Service Act as it is at present worded. Some hon. gentlemen opposite have said we do not need a committee because we had one two years ago. Do those hon. gentlemen not know that for five years-more than that, for perhaps seven years-year after year, session after session, we had a committee on Pensions and Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment which revised, reviewed and amended the Pension Act, the act with regard to the re-establishment on the land and several other statutes? Surely it is no worse to amend the Civil Service Act than it was to amend an act which dealt with a far more important matter, that of the welfare and well-being of our soldiers who had fought overseas.
Another view of the situation has been taken by my hon. friend for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) and in order to reassure him I will ask the Prime Minister, or rather the chief Whip not to appoint me on the committee. I do not know, though, why he does not carry his argument to its logical conclusion and retire from the House, or request the electors of Quebec South to ask me to retire. However, for the sake of peace and harmony, I am willing to ask the chief Whip on the government side not to appoint me one of the members of the committee. I hope that will meet the view of the hon. member for Lisgar, that it will answer some of his objections, that he will see to it that he is confirmed in his desire to do the fair thing by the Civil Service Act, by the government, and by this House, and that he will vote in favour, at least, of referring the stud}' of this matter to a committee.

speechtext: The House having reverted to the order, "Motions":

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO PREPARE SCHEDULES
speechtext:
I wish now to move the committee to which is to be referred the bill for the readjustment of the constituencies. I made mention yesterday to the House that the government were of the opinion that a small committee was advisable rather than a large one; that it should consist of possibly eleven members at the outset, certainly not more than fifteen. However, it has been represented by my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) that some injustice would be done his group if it were not represented by four members on the committee, in which event, following out the proportionate representation in the House, it would be necessary to have a committee as large as nineteen. Now, the government is anxious in this matter of redistribution that there shall not be so much even as the shadow of an impression that anything is being attempted other than what is reasonable and just in all particulars. The government wishes U>
avoid anything in the nature of party controversy if possible, and under the circumstances we propose to 'meet hon. gentlemen opposite and grant a committee of nineteen. I would therefore move:	[DOT]
That Bill No. 15, intituled An Act to readjust the representation of the House of Commons, be referred to a special committee consisting of Messrs. Beland, Boivin, Caldwell, Euler, Hanson, Johnston, Low, Kennedy (Glengarry Stormont), King (Huron), Macdonald (Pictou), Me Murray, McQuarrie, Morrissy, Motherwell, Speakman, Stewart (Argenteuil), Stewart (Leeds), Stork and Sutherland, with instructions, to prepare schedules to contain and describe the several electoral divisions entitled to return members to this House and to report the same and that Rule 11 be suspended in relation thereto.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO PREPARE SCHEDULES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take this occasion to discuss one of the principles that I think should be had in mind in the consideration of this question, namely, representation by population and the distribution of the seats on that basis. The British North America Act, section 51, says:
On the completion of the census in the year one thousand eight hundred and seventy-one, and of each subsequent decennial census, the representation of the four provinces shall be readjusted by such authority, in such a manner, and from such time as the parliament of Canada from time to time provides, subject and according to the following rules:-
[M r. McQuarrie.]
(1)	Quebec shall have the fixed number of sixty-five
members;	*
(2)	There shall be assigned to each of the other provinces such a number of members as will bear the same proportion to the number of its population (ascertained at such census) as the number sixty-five bears to the number of the population of Quebec (so ascertained) ;
(3)	In the computation of the number of members for a province a fractional part not exceeding one half of the whole number requisite for entitling the province to a member shall be disregarded; but a fractional part exceeding one half of that number shall be equivalent to the whole number;
(4)	On any such readjustment the number of members for a province shall not be reduced unless the proportion which the number of the population of the province bore to the number of the aggregate population of Canada at the then last preceding readjustment of the number of members for the province is ascertained at the then latest census to be diminished by one twentieth part or upwards:
(5)	Such readjustment shall not take effect until the termination of the then existing parliament.
52. The number of members of the House of Commons may be from time to time increased by the parliament of Canada, provided the proportionate representation of the provinces prescribed by this act is not thereby disturbed.
The point I wish to make, Mr. Speaker, is that population is the basis of readjustment not only as between the provinces but also as to the subdivision of the various seats within the provinces. The constitution of this country, in the provisions that I have read, provides that redistribution shall recognize the principle of representation by population and nothing else. But strangely enough, since this act came into force we have had several redistributions all of which have clearly ignored the law in this respect. Take my own case: according to the last census, the figures of which I have under my hand, I represent a population of over 100.000. At the last redistribution it was a little over thirty thousand. Now as a matter of fact, these one hundred thousand people are out-voted by five other constituencies in this country whose members represent less than twenty thousand people.

subtopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO PREPARE SCHEDULES
speechtext:
(York): They come out and vote just as much as the people in any other portion of this country, and sixty thousand of them have the right to register now, including women. I say that if this is a democratic country, one man's vote is as good as another man's, but as it is now there is an

Redistribution
unfair discrimination against the urban vote in favour of the rural vote. Why that should be I do not know. I could read out a list of twenty-one constituencies to illustrate my point, but here is the fact. Toronto and Montreal together have almost one-fifth the population of this country, but they have not anything like the representation that the rural parts have, or the representation that I say they are entitled to have under the constitution. I therefore take this occasion of insisting in so far as I can upon the recognition of this principle that the value of votes in this country should be absolutely on an equality based on population. I think I am backed in that by the Prime Minister and by the Progressives from the West who absolutely admit this democratic principle, and recognizing that principle, I think the House also must recognize it.
What is the history of this question? I could go back over the thirty years I have been in the House, and still further back to other redistributions. In the first election I ran I was a supporter of Sir John A. Macdonald. I knew Sir John A. Macdonald and at that time'he was trying to cultivate the votes of the cities of this country in favour of his National policy, but he never went the length of telling the people at that time that one man's vote was as good as another's, and that the cities and towns should have equal representation and influence in this House with the rural sections of the countiy. After him came Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and he also for some reason or other refused to recognize the principle of equality of representation, not only as between constituencies, but also as between individual voters, and this principle of equality was ignored. Since then the population of this country has been growing, particularly of Ontario and Quebec, so that to-day the urban population in both these provinces exceeds the rural population, and yet they have not anything like the same representation in this House. In other words, there are twenly-one or twenty-three constituencies where less than twenty thousand voters have the representation that is accorded to my constituency with one hundred thousand people.
As pointed out by the Prime Minister in his address, the unit of representation, which . is based on the population of
12 m. the province of Quebec divided by sixty-five, will be thirty-six thousand under this redistribution according to the last census, and that is the basis upon which the redistribution should be done. That is what I am insisting on here, and so far as any discussion has taken place in this House,
I can claim that I have the acceptance by the Prime Minister of the old principle of representation by population. I am quite sure that the Progressives from the West also, while it may be said that the rural population ought perhaps to be entitled to a little more representation, will admit the absolute correctness of the principle of equality. How can we ever have a democratic government in this country unless we absolutely recognize the principle of equality of representation as between citizens and as between constituencies?
Therefore I make this contention, and I ask the House and the committee to admit this principle in the new distribution, so that this discrimination as against the urban population in favour of the rural population will not be continued. It never should have happened. It does not obtain in any other democratic country in the world. This principle on which I insist absolutely governs the representation in congress in the United States, and there is a much fairer representation in the British parliament to-day where the value of votes in the cities and rural parts is the same, than we have in this country. The same rule obtains in all the British Commonwealths except Canada, where for some reason or other, partly through inadvertence, partly by a mistake in the past, partly because we started wrong, this injustice has not been righted, I stand in my place to-day on behalf of the urban population of this country and ask the committee to recognize the justice of this principle of equality being applied not only to the representation apportioned to provinces but also to the constituencies that will be defined.
I admit, if it has to be admitted-I do not think I should admit it-that it might be unfair at the present time to apply the change too strictly, I would be prepared to still give the rural constituencies some advantage on the understanding that eventually the principle of the equality of values shall be strictly applied to constituencies as it is now applied to the provinces. If there must be and there ought to be in every democratic country this equality, I say now is the time to make the change.
I quoted in this House the other day the attitude of some of our politicians in the past, and pointed out that William Lyon Mackenzie in the old, old days in this country, was in favour of representation by population. The Hon. George Brown was in favour of it also. The Liberal party favoured the principle, and I never heard of the party going back upon it when the question came up. But gradually in the readjustments we have had, and the four or five reconsiderations of this question, we have allowed ourselves to go
Redistribution

wrong, and to be unfair, and to-day we are unfair to a majority of the population; because, if you look up the census you will see that the majority of the population in both Ontario and Quebec is urban, as against rural. If that is the case, now is the time to make a change, and, on behalf of the great cities of Toronto and Montreal, and of the towns and smaller cities in every province in Canada,
I ask that we begin to correct this mistake and to adopt the principle as we have adopted it as between provinces in the creation of constituencies in the respective provinces. I am sure I can appeal, in making this contention, to the fairness of all the parties of this House, Liberals, Conservatives, Progressives and Independents, and I expect that we shall have to-night an expression of opinion from the government and other members of the House as to whether they are of opinion that representation by population from now on should govern in every measure of redistribution that may be brought into this House, and that the constitution be respected and observed. I have read from the British North America Act, and I cannot find in any of the amending acts any alteration in the law set out in the sections I have quoted.
I leave the matter for the present, but will follow it up on some other occasion, perhaps . before the committee, but I ask for some expression to-night from this House as to whether it is not time we should make this change and adopt the great democratic principle that one man's vote is as good as another, and that the value of a vote in one constituency ought to be the same as the value of the vote in any other constituency in the Dominion of Canada.

Motion agreed to.
